rationale: Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all abdominal aortic aneurysm), method (PRS-CS), variant count (1,118,997), and ancestry context (GWAS AFR+EUR; EUR evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model metrics are only weakly informative. In that setting, PGS003973 has cleaner disclosed basic covariate adjustment (age, age^2, sex) and reports a substantially higher full-model discrimination (C-index 0.882 with CI) than PGS003972’s AUROC 0.69 with unknown covariates, making PGS003973 the better-supported record despite the limited PRS-only comparability.

PGS001267 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait (ankylosing spondylitis) with a direct disease phenotype (“Ankylosing spondylitis” / phenotyping_reported: “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly time-to-event (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)” / phenotyping_reported: “TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. The two records are otherwise near-clones (same pan-trait UKB framework paper, same snpnet method, same 10 variants, same training/validation sizes, same covariates, same ancestry distribution). Although PGS001268 shows slightly higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346 vs 0.7265; PGS-only R² 0.1023 vs 0.0988), the difference is small and does not outweigh the endpoint-alignment advantage of PGS001267.

PGS002727 is a disease-focused score explicitly targeting pediatric asthma (phenotyping_reported: "Pediatric asthma") from a dedicated asthma paper, with supportive effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.57) and very large external evaluation (n=391,820) across multiple ancestries, suggesting robustness beyond a single-cohort setting. PGS001782 comes from a global biobank portability/framework-style paper and is evaluated only in EUR; while it reports a clean PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2 (0.048844, below the asthma h2_liability ceiling) and similar AUROC (~0.659), that metric advantage is modest and does not clearly outweigh the framework penalty and narrower evaluation context. Given comparable discrimination signals but stronger endpoint-focused study archetype and effect-size support, PGS002727 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper, with identical training cohort (UKB), training N (269,704), covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (24,905 EUR selected). The main differentiator is endpoint fidelity: PGS001260 uses a generic angina phenotype (“Angina” / phenotyping_reported: “Angina”), which better matches the target trait (angina pectoris) than PGS001261’s time-to-event framing (“Angina pectoris (time-to-event)” / “TTE angina pectoris”), which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease target. Performance differences slightly favor PGS001261 (PGS-only AUROC 0.58233 vs 0.58108; PGS-only R2 0.01228 vs 0.01185), but the gap is tiny and both are plausible under the heritability ceiling, so endpoint alignment is the more defensible tie-break here.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size evidence, structural properties, and transportability context. PGS002738 shows a stronger reported discrimination signal (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (OR 1.76 [1.32–2.34]) and is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858 gene-based variants), which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal for complex traits. While PGS002739 is evaluated in AFR (useful for African-ancestry deployment), its much sparser gene-based construction and weaker OR make it less likely to rank higher on a generic external benchmark than the stronger, genome-wide PGS002738.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo alcoholic liver cirrhosis) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC is not a reliable differentiator across studies. PGS001777 is from a disease-focused study explicitly about predicting alcohol-related cirrhosis in drinkers and shows much stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18; beta 1.132), whereas PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics framework paper and shows only a modest HR per SD (1.18), suggesting weaker standalone PRS discrimination despite its larger genome-wide model. Given endpoint fidelity plus materially stronger effect-size evidence, PGS001777 is better-supported for external performance on alcoholic liver cirrhosis.

PGS004587 is better aligned to the target trait as a general atopic eczema/atopic dermatitis endpoint (phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis), whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype (moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis), which is a meaningful endpoint restriction for a generic “atopic eczema” target. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics with covariates (including parental ethnicity) and are not comparable PRS evidence and are also implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling, suggesting covariate-driven performance. PGS004587 at least provides a PRS-stratified HR (1.153 high vs low) in a large EUR evaluation (n=337,910) with non-clinical covariates, making it the more externally plausible, endpoint-faithful choice despite being sparse (23 SNPs).

PGS004913 is a disease-focused score explicitly developed for alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis among heavy drinkers, with phenotype fields tightly aligned to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both alcohol-associated cirrhosis) and it reports a strong PRS stratification effect (OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4). PGS000704, while label-aligned, comes from a broad biomarker genetics UKB framework context and only provides a full-model time-to-event C-index (0.711) plus a modest per-SD HR (1.18), with no PRS-only metrics; its apparent performance is likely more covariate-driven and less endpoint-optimized for cirrhosis risk prediction. Despite PGS000704’s much larger training/validation and genome-wide variant count, the endpoint-focused design and stronger effect-size evidence favor PGS004913 for expected external benchmark ranking.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable PRS metrics. PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is heavily discounted because its covariates include the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF, a strong packaging/leakage signal that can dominate discrimination and obscures the standalone PRS contribution. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), making its reported evidence more interpretable for PRS quality, and it also shows a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.82) alongside a cross-ancestry PRS-CSx construction with much larger genome-wide variant coverage (1.27M vs 0.38M). Despite a smaller validation N, the cleaner covariate design plus strong OR and structurally stronger cross-ancestry method support PGS005313 as more likely to transfer well.

PGS001135 is better-supported on comparable PRS evidence: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.539 and PRS-only R²=0.00291 (with CI for AUROC) under basic covariates, and these values are sanity-consistent with the low heritability ceiling noted for arthritis. It also includes multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. In contrast, PGS004477 provides no PRS-comparable performance metrics (AUC/R² all null) and only a modest OR=1.20 with unknown covariates, plus EUR-only evaluation; despite its genome-wide LDpred2 construction and large variant count, the lack of directly comparable validation performance makes it less well-supported for ranking here.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis: it has direct trait alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo both aortic stenosis) with the same incident aortic stenosis endpoint and identical basic covariates/ancestry/validation context as PGS005255. With endpoints and study family effectively near-clone, the tie-break is comparative evidence of PRS strength: PGS005254 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53) and is trained on a larger sample (205,483 vs 98,645), while variant counts and method (PRS-CS) are essentially the same and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. Therefore PGS005254 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking.

PGS001262 and PGS001261 are near-clone snpnet scores from the same UKB pan-trait framework paper with identical covariates and very similar ancestry evaluation context, so PRS-only metrics are a fair tie-break. PGS001262 has slightly better PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.58683 vs 0.58233; PGS-only R2 0.01304 vs 0.01228) and a larger validation sample (49,472 vs 24,905). Endpoint-wise, PGS001262 uses a direct doctor-diagnosed angina phenotype, whereas PGS001261 is explicitly time-to-event (a mild endpoint penalty for a generic angina pectoris target). Both R2 values are below the heritability ceiling, so the small edge for PGS001262 is credible.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO mapping (arthritis), same publication, same EUR-only DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (UKB), same training N and validation N, same variant count, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and have unknown covariates. With metrics unavailable, the main differentiator is the available effect-size signal and structural method cue: PGS004547 reports a higher OR per SD (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), and its method (RFDiseasemetaPRS) is an explicit meta/aggregation-style construction which is generally a positive structural signal versus a single-score LDpred2 sibling when other fields are identical. Therefore PGS004547 is better-supported here.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint alignment is tighter: trait_efo is exactly "alcohol dependence" and both trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are Alcohol use disorder (a near-synonymous clinical diagnosis construct). It is also developed from a more disease-focused multi-cohort context (MVP/PGC/UKB) and uses a cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with evaluation in African American samples, suggesting intentional transportability beyond a single-biobank EUR-only setup. While neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS002739 provides a reasonably strong discrimination signal via OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76, whereas PGS000201’s main comparable metric is a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192 and it is trained/evaluated EUR-only in UKB with covariate-heavy adjustment, making its evidence less directly indicative of standalone PRS strength for alcohol dependence.

Both candidates match the target trait well (AAA; same EFO), but PGS003972 is structurally far better supported as a modern genome-wide PRS (PRS-CS with 1,118,997 variants) developed in a large multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis context, which is typically more predictive than a very sparse P+T score. PGS000753 uses only 29 variants (P+T) and, while it reports a moderate OR=1.37 per SD, it lacks any discrimination metrics and is based on a smaller, older MVP-focused architecture; its larger validation N does not compensate for the sparse construction. PGS003972’s reported AUROC=0.69 is full-model (not PRS-only) and covariates are unknown, so the metric advantage is discounted, but the combination of disease-focused multi-biobank development plus genome-wide shrinkage/variant coverage makes it more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the 29-variant score.

PGS001135 has directly comparable PRS-only performance reported for arthritis (PGS-only AUROC=0.539, PGS-only R2=0.00291) with basic covariates and a clear evaluation record, allowing sanity-checking against the (low) heritability ceiling and indicating a weak but quantified PRS signal. PGS004547 is more endpoint-specific (“M13 Other arthritis”) and uses a genome-wide/metaPRS-style method with many variants, but it provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 at all (only an OR=1.26 with unknown covariates), making its predictive strength and comparability much less supported on the visible fields despite the larger validation N.

PGS004913 is better supported as a standalone PRS for the target endpoint: its phenotyping_reported and trait_reported both directly match alcohol-associated cirrhosis, and it uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) without obvious clinical-risk packaging. It is also a more polygenic construction (20 variants via PRSice-2) with a strong reported stratification effect (OR top vs bottom deciles 4.4). In contrast, PGS001777 is an extremely sparse 3-variant “genetic risk score” from a paper explicitly combining genetics with diabetes prediction; it reports only a full-model AUROC (0.671) with unknown covariates (not PRS-comparable) and its phenotyping_reported is restricted to “Cirrhosis (males),” reducing endpoint fidelity/generalizability for the generic alcoholic liver cirrhosis target.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is a direct clinical diagnosis construct (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence), whereas PGS000201 is framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with an EFO mapping to an alcohol-dependence *measurement*, making endpoint fidelity weaker/less direct. Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on the preferred metrics; in that setting, PGS002738 has stronger discriminative evidence via a sizable OR for top 10% vs rest (1.96, 95% CI 1.54–2.51) compared with PGS000201’s small incremental ΔR² (0.01192) and modest beta. Both are EUR-evaluated with similar validation N (~7.9k vs ~7.6k) and same method family (PRS-CS), so the decision is driven mainly by the more diagnosis-faithful phenotype and stronger effect-size signal in PGS002738.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/C-index is not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS005168 is heavily packaged with a named clinical risk calculator covariate (CHARGE-AF) in addition to age/sex/array, making its high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and discounted for standalone PRS quality; its effect size (HR per SD 1.67) is strong but not isolated from that packaging context. PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding risk-calculator leakage, and shows a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.94) that is more interpretable as PRS signal; despite being a sparser P+T score and EAS-only evaluation, the cleaner covariate design and stronger effect-size evidence make it the better-supported PRS candidate here.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) and very large genome-wide variant coverage (985,837), plus a strong reported PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.57), and broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS). Although it lacks clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (only full-model AUROC=0.66, R²=0.04), its endpoint is explicitly pediatric asthma and the study archetype is asthma-specific. In contrast, PGS001344 comes from the pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework (a known weaker-transfer archetype) with a much smaller SNP set (6,139); while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.6457, R² 0.0597) under basic covariates and these are below the asthma heritability ceiling, the framework/sparse-model context and narrower development (UKB EUR-only) make it less likely to generalize as well as the disease-focused, genome-wide PRS-CS pediatric asthma score.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it is explicitly labeled and mapped to aortic stenosis and uses an incident aortic stenosis endpoint, whereas PGS005255 is framed as “Mean pressure gradient” with mixed EFO mapping (“aortic stenosis, aortic measurement”), making endpoint fidelity less direct despite also mentioning incident aortic stenosis. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size and design signals matter more; PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting stronger standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252 reports a high full-model C-index (0.87), it uses many clinical covariates (comorbidities and BMI/smoking), so that metric is not PRS-comparable; still, the stronger HR and cleaner trait alignment outweigh PGS005255’s larger training N and simpler covariates, which are weak differentiators here.

PGS002755 is the better-supported standalone PRS for atopic eczema: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and is evaluated at large scale in EUR (n=337,910), with a PRS-derived effect size reported (HR high vs low PRS=1.249). PGS001773 targets a narrower endpoint (moderate-to-severe AD) and is a very sparse 25-variant score in a small evaluation (n=676); its headline AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics with demographic/ethnicity covariates and are not PRS-only, and the R² is implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.071), suggesting the performance is largely covariate/packaging-driven rather than PRS signal. Despite PGS002755 being from a cross-disease comparison paper and lacking PRS-only AUC/R², its endpoint is closer to generic atopic eczema and its structural/scale evidence is more consistent with external benchmark performance than the covariate-inflated small-cohort result in PGS001773.

PGS002089 has cleaner endpoint fidelity for the target (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are plain ankylosing spondylitis), uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026 SNPs), and comes from a portability-focused evaluation explicitly spanning multiple ancestries (EUR/GME/SAS in evaluation), which is supportive for transfer. PGS001268 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R² (AUROC 0.7346; R² 0.1023) but is from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant snpnet model and a time-to-event phenotype framing, both of which are warning signals for generalization despite the cleaner metrics. With no directly comparable PRS-only metrics for PGS002089, confidence is low, but the structural/method and endpoint advantages favor PGS002089 over the sparse framework score.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with the same trait_efo (angina pectoris), similar basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and the same DEV/EVAL ancestry distribution, so endpoint fidelity and transportability context do not differentiate them meaningfully. In this same-family setting, PRS-comparable metrics are a legitimate tie-break: PGS001262 has slightly better PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.58683 vs 0.58108; PGS-only R2 0.01304 vs 0.01185) and higher incremental AUROC (0.0098 vs 0.00783) than PGS001260. Although PGS001260 has more variants and larger training N, those are weaker signals here and do not outweigh the consistently stronger PRS-only metrics for PGS001262; both R2 values remain plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis) and only basic demographic/PC-style covariates, so phenotype/covariate fidelity is essentially tied. PGS001267 has cleaner PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.7265; PGS-only R2 0.0988), but it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant model, a pattern that domain guidance flags as often generalizing poorly despite complete metrics. PGS002089 is also a UKB framework/portability paper, but it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026) and shows nontrivial PRS signal via partial-r=0.0919; it is also evaluated across multiple ancestries (EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for transfer. Given the benchmark objective (likely external performance/robustness), the structural advantage (LDpred2 + much larger variant set) outweighs the metric-format advantage of the sparse snpnet score, but the lack of directly comparable PRS-only AUROC/R2 for PGS002089 keeps confidence low.

Both candidates match the target well (aortic stenosis; incident cases; EUR dev/eval) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size evidence and design comparability. PGS005252 reports only a covariate-heavy full-model C-index/AUC=0.87 (age/sex/PCs plus multiple comorbidities and risk factors), which is not PRS-comparable and is likely largely covariate-driven; its HR=1.92 lacks a CI. PGS005254 uses much cleaner/basic covariates (age, age^2, sex, PCs) and reports an HR=1.64 with CI (1.50–1.78), giving more interpretable PRS-specific evidence without clinical-variable inflation. Despite PGS005252 having a larger evaluation N and slightly higher point HR, the covariate leakage risk and non-comparable full-model metric make PGS005254 the better-supported standalone PRS candidate.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported incident atopic dermatitis), use the same evaluation ancestry (EUR) and identical covariates, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so metrics don’t differentiate cleanly. In that setting, structural signals dominate: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to polygenic disease prediction than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNP score. The available effect-size evidence is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR high vs low PRS 1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587 lists multiple training cohorts, but its study is framed around air pollution/elderly-onset risk and the very sparse SNP set is a weaker standalone PRS package than the genome-wide PRS-CS score.

PGS001782 is better-supported for external benchmark performance because it comes from a global multi-biobank, multi-ancestry development context (many cohorts listed) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (884,043), which is structurally favored for a polygenic disease like asthma and typically transfers better than sparse pan-trait UKB scores. Although PGS001344 reports slightly higher PRS-only metrics in EUR (PGS-only R2 0.0597; AUROC 0.6457) than PGS001782’s covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only R2 0.0488, PGS001344 is explicitly from the ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet framework (UKB-only development, 6,139 variants), a study archetype that domain guidance flags as systematically weaker in external generalization. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (doctor-diagnosed vs generic asthma), covariates are similarly basic, and both R2 values are below the asthma heritability ceiling; thus the framework penalty and stronger method/coverage/study archetype for PGS001782 outweigh the modest metric edge of PGS001344.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all AF) and both only report full-model AUROC (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the AUROC values (0.78 for PGS005313 vs 0.74 for PGS002814) are not strongly comparable. Given that, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS005313 uses a genome-wide cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with ~1.27M variants and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (selected_validation_ancestry includes European, African, South Asian, East Asian, Hispanic/LatAm), which is stronger evidence for external robustness than PGS002814’s sparse P+T score (4,520 variants) evaluated only in East Asians. Covariates are basic in both (age/sex; PGS002814 adds PCs), so no major leakage difference. Overall, PGS005313 is better-supported for broad external performance/benchmark ranking, while PGS002814’s large training N and reported pseudo-R2 do not compensate for the sparser method and single-ancestry evaluation context.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003973 is better-supported structurally and by study context: it is a disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis score using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is generally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T 29-variant PGS000753. Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model C-index=0.882 for PGS003973 (age/age^2/sex) cannot be treated as PRS-comparable, but it is at least consistent with a standard demographic-adjusted evaluation. PGS000753’s main quantitative support is an OR per SD of 1.37 (moderate) and it uses a prevalent endpoint, with no discrimination metrics; despite its larger validation N and some multi-ancestry evaluation, the extreme sparsity and weaker effect-size evidence make it less likely to rank highest in external benchmarks than the genome-wide PRS-CS model.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/study family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only ancestry across GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and size (n=11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same validation size (n=11,322), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). With endpoint and design effectively tied, the only visible differentiator is slightly stronger performance/effect evidence for PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher OR for top 1% vs rest (3.79 vs 3.61), while AUROC is identical (0.632). Given the tiny differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, confidence is low but PGS000454 has the slight edge.

PGS001263 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint fidelity is exact across fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial flutter), whereas PGS001339 explicitly targets a broader composite and different endpoint framing ("atrial fibrillation and flutter" with time-to-event phenotyping and dual EFO mapping), which is a mismatch for a pure atrial flutter target. Both are near-clones otherwise (same snpnet method, same UKB-only training n=269,704, same basic covariates, same validation n=24,905, same framework paper), so PRS-only metrics can be used as a tie-break: PGS001263 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC (0.61716 vs 0.613) and PRS-only R2 (0.02517 vs 0.02447), with both R2 values plausibly below the local h2_obs ceiling. The performance differences are small, but combined with the cleaner phenotype alignment they favor PGS001263.

Both candidates are near-clones: same basal cell carcinoma endpoint (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping all match), same publication/family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same training and validation sample sizes, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this same-context comparison, PGS000454 has a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0489 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456 has marginally higher top-1% OR (3.95 vs 3.79). Given the tiny metric differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, the edge is weak; I pick PGS000454 on the slightly better overall discrimination/pseudo-R² in the matched setting.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size/cohort (UKB n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either and essentially identical partial correlation (partial-r=0.0716 with overlapping CIs), performance evidence does not differentiate. The main remaining structural signal is method/coverage: PGS002032 uses LDpred2 with 19,768 variants (genome-wide shrinkage), which is generally better supported for capturing polygenic signal than the very sparse penalized regression score in PGS001824 with only 22 variants, especially within the same publication family and identical endpoint/covariates.

Both candidates target the same combined endpoint (atrial fibrillation and flutter) and are UKB-derived with broadly similar basic covariate adjustment and multi-ancestry evaluation listings. Candidate_a (PGS001339) provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.613; PGS-only R2 0.0245) that are plausible vs the heritability ceiling, but it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (2,142 variants), which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly. Candidate_b (PGS002050) is also a framework/portability-style UKB paper, but uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (554,908 variants) and larger training N, which is a stronger structural signal for a polygenic cardiac arrhythmia endpoint when direct PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. Because PGS002050 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only partial-r reported), confidence is low, but the method/coverage advantage over the sparse snpnet framework score makes it more likely to rank higher externally.

PGS001263 is a direct endpoint match to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), with basic covariates and an R² that is plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling context. PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”), and while it has a larger genome-wide model (LDpred2; 554,908 variants) and larger training N, it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² and reports only partial correlation, making its predictive strength for atrial flutter specifically less directly supported on the visible fields. Given both are UKB framework-style scores, the decisive visible advantage is PGS001263’s exact phenotype alignment plus explicit PRS-only metrics.

PGS001033 has direct endpoint alignment to the target (trait_efo = blood coagulation disease; phenotyping_reported = other coagulation defects) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.634 and PGS-only R² 0.0578) with only basic covariates, plus broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS). In contrast, PGS002034 targets a narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency subtype (trait_efo = congenital vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors deficiency) rather than the broad blood coagulation disease umbrella, and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a modest partial-r 0.0563), making its predictive strength less directly supported despite a genome-wide LDpred2 build.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), covariates, training size, and ancestry distribution/evaluation context, and they show essentially identical partial-r performance (0.0563 vs 0.0562). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes to separate them, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002034 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (32,552 variants) versus PGS001826’s very sparse penalized regression score (45 variants). Given the same endpoint and evaluation setting, the higher-coverage shrinkage model is better-supported to capture polygenic signal and thus more likely to rank higher externally.
