Both candidates align well to the target COPD concept (same trait_reported/trait_efo; minor phenotyping wording difference with PGS001332). However, PGS001788 shows materially stronger PRS-comparable performance (covariates-regressed-out/PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.0163) than PGS001332’s PGS-only R2=0.00235 and only modest PGS-only AUROC=0.5397, with PGS001332’s higher full-model AUROC likely largely covariate-driven (incremental AUROC only 0.003). PGS001788 also has stronger structural support for a polygenic disease (PRS-CS-auto with ~910k variants) versus PGS001332’s very sparse snpnet score (482 variants) from a pan-trait UKB framework paper, which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external transfer. Although PGS001332 has explicit PGS-only AUROC and multi-ancestry evaluation records, its PRS-only signal is weak; overall the multi-biobank PRS-CS-auto score with higher PRS-only R2 is better-supported.

PGS005170 is better supported for the target trait dementia because it is explicitly built for all-cause dementia with matching phenotyping (incident all-cause dementia) and uses a much stronger structural approach (integrative ensemble of 24 component PRSs with genome-wide methods; 1,320,229 variants) versus PGS000823’s very sparse genome-wide-significant 23-variant score. While neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS005170 at least reports an HR per SD (1.25) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation (including non-EUR groups), whereas PGS000823 reports only a tertile HR contrast (1.36 top vs bottom) and is evaluated only in EUR. PGS005170’s covariates include APOE allele dosage (a potential inflation/packaging concern), but PGS000823’s sparse construction and lack of PRS-comparable metrics make it less likely to rank highly in external benchmarks for dementia.

PGS004951 is the better-supported match to the target trait (dilated cardiomyopathy) because its phenotyping_reported is the direct clinical endpoint (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”), whereas PGS004949 is explicitly restricted to a subtype (“Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy”), which is a fidelity mismatch for a generic DCM target. Performance evidence is broadly similar between the siblings (PRS-only AUC ~0.67 vs 0.68; OR per SD 1.93 vs 1.91; similar beta/SE), so the small AUC/OR differences don’t outweigh endpoint alignment. Additionally, PGS004951’s evaluation is in EUR (matching the provided EUR heritability context), while PGS004949 is evaluated in MAE-only, making its reported metrics less directly comparable/transferable to a typical EUR benchmark setting despite its larger validation N and slightly higher full-model R2.

Both candidates target dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG) with PRS-CS and only basic covariates, but PGS004949 provides cleaner PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a univariate (PRS-only) AUC of 0.68 (with CI) and delta PRS/residual R² metrics, whereas PGS004862 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) which are not directly comparable as PRS-only. PGS004949 also shows slightly stronger effect size (OR 1.91 vs 1.76) and higher variant count (1,038,394 vs 709,534), supporting stronger polygenic capture. Although PGS004862 has a more directly matched evaluation ancestry (EUR vs MAE-only evaluation for PGS004949) and slightly larger validation N, the presence of PRS-only metrics plus stronger OR/variant count makes PGS004949 better-supported overall.

PGS004281 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia on endpoint fidelity: it is explicitly "All-cause dementia" with trait_efo="dementia" and phenotyping_reported="All-cause dementia", whereas PGS000823 is framed as "Alzheimer's disease" (trait_efo="Alzheimer disease") despite phenotyping_reported being incident all-cause dementia, creating a concept/endpoint mismatch for a generic dementia target. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004281’s reported full-model AUROC (~0.819) cannot be treated as PRS performance but is at least based on basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a large EUR evaluation (n=67,428). PGS000823 is a very sparse 23-variant GWS score with only a modest HR (1.36 top vs bottom tertile) and no training N, making its standalone PRS signal look weaker than the more polygenic 110-variant score in PGS004281.

PGS004614 is the better-supported diverticular disease PRS because it comes from a clearly disease-focused GWAS paper on diverticular disease and provides at least some discrimination evidence (AUROC 0.76), whereas PGS004544 comes from a more generic “risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration” framework with no AUC/R2 reported at all (only an OR=1.32, which is moderate). Although PGS004614’s AUROC is a full-model metric and is likely inflated by explicit family history covariate inclusion (reducing PRS-only comparability), PGS004544 has unknown covariates and lacks any comparable PRS performance metric, making its support weaker overall. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both map to diverticular disease; PGS004544 is ICD10 K57), so the decision turns on study archetype and available performance evidence, favoring PGS004614.

PGS004621 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all generic “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (trait_efo alcoholic liver cirrhosis), a narrower subtype and thus a weaker endpoint match for the broad target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/C-index are not decisive and are not directly comparable across differing designs; however PGS004621 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.42 vs HR 1.18 for PGS000704), suggesting more PRS signal. Study archetype/transportability also favors PGS004621: it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort cirrhosis genetics study with many contributing cohorts and very large validation (EUR), while PGS000704 is from a broader UKB biomarker genetics framework with single-cohort development and mixed EUR/MAE evaluation. Covariates are similarly basic in both, so they don’t rescue the subtype mismatch in PGS000704.

Both candidates target the same trait framing (Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG), EFO dilated cardiomyopathy) and use the same method (PRS-CS) with EUR-only evaluation, so the decision hinges on endpoint fidelity and PRS-attributable performance evidence. PGS004951 has slightly stronger endpoint specificity via phenotyping_reported="Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy" (vs PGS004862 "Dilated cardiomyopathy") and, critically, it reports an explicit PRS-only discrimination metric (Univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI) plus delta PRS/residual R² metrics, giving direct evidence of PRS contribution; PGS004862 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.71/0.05) which is not PRS-comparable and could be covariate-driven. Effect-size support is also stronger for PGS004951 (OR 1.93 vs 1.76). Although PGS004862 has a much larger validation sample (347,585 vs 7,761) and includes age/sex covariates, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not compensate for the lack of PRS-only metrics. Overall, PGS004951 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for the target endpoint.

PGS004614 is the stronger choice because it comes from a disease-focused diverticular disease GWAS/prediction study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (SBayesR) with very large variant coverage (1,082,282), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse snpnet framework score in PGS000997 (5,757 variants) from the pan-trait “813 traits in UK Biobank” paper. Although PGS000997 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591, R2 0.0178) that are heritability-plausible, it is also a time-to-event endpoint and a known framework archetype that tends to generalize worse than disease-specific models. PGS004614 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC 0.76 with covariates including family history, making it non-comparable), which lowers confidence, but its endpoint is a direct diverticular disease diagnosis and its study/method/coverage package is more consistent with better external benchmark performance than the sparse UKB framework score.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to major depressive disorder (same EFO; phenotyping_reported is depression/MDD) and both are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL with similar genome-wide PRS-CS-style methods and ~1.09M variants, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. The key differentiator is that PGS002759 provides a directly interpretable PRS effect size (OR per SD = 1.26, 95% CI 1.22–1.30) under basic covariate adjustment (age, sex, PCs, technical), giving cleaner PRS-specific evidence of discrimination, whereas PGS003333 reports only a small full-model/Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 (0.022) with covariates unknown and no effect size, making its PRS contribution harder to assess. Validation sample sizes are similar (39,444 vs 34,703) and do not outweigh the stronger PRS-specific evidence in PGS002759.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo major depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported is MDD), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show small full-model/unspecified R2 ~0.022–0.024, which is not strongly comparable). PGS003333 is better-supported structurally and by study archetype: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) built from multi-cohort depression GWAS sources (23andMe/PGC/UKB), which is typically more robust for a highly polygenic disorder than the PRSice-2 clumping/thresholding approach in PGS003576. While PGS003576 has broader evaluation ancestries and slightly higher reported R2, it is trained/developed only in UKB and the metric difference is tiny and likely not meaningful given differing covariate disclosure (PGS003576 adjusts PCs 1–10; PGS003333 covariates unknown). Overall, the multi-cohort disease-GWAS basis plus stronger method family favors PGS003333.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful for coronary artery disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all CAD) and use the same method family (LDpred) with essentially identical genome-wide variant counts (~6.6M), so the decision turns on strength/recency of evidence and transportability. PGS002244 comes from a large cross-ancestry, million-person study with broader multi-ancestry evaluation (explicit AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS evaluation) and larger training/validation (175,364 train; 343,676 eval) plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.64, 95% CI 1.61–1.67), which is a strong PRS-quality signal even without AUC/R2. PGS000013 reports a PRS-comparable Nagelkerke R2=0.04 (below the CAD heritability ceiling, so plausible), but its headline AUROC=0.81 is full-model (not PRS-only) and thus not a clean cross-model discriminator; it also has smaller training/validation (120,280 train; 288,978 eval). Given similar covariate cleanliness (basic demographics/PCs/array) and near-clone construction, the stronger effect-size evidence and broader multi-ancestry evaluation context favor PGS002244 over PGS000013.

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000644 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the follicular lymphoma EFO, creating endpoint-fidelity ambiguity. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are only weakly comparable; still, PGS002304 shows higher reported AUROC (0.61 vs 0.538). Although PGS000644 has a more polygenic construction (lassosum; ~2.2M variants) and basic covariates disclosed, its effect-size evidence is modest (OR per SD ~1.15; top 1% OR 1.48 with wide CI) and does not outweigh the stronger phenotype alignment plus better observed discrimination in PGS002304.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity to Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and direct disease phenotyping). PGS001254 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.6646; PGS R2 0.0247) but comes from the pan-trait UKB sparse PRS framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely small variant set (11), a known pattern that often generalizes poorly. PGS002092 is also a UKB framework/portability paper, but uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (~484k) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for robustness/transfer even though it lacks directly comparable PRS-only AUC/R2. Given the structural advantage (method + genome-wide coverage) and broader evaluation context, PGS002092 is more likely to rank higher externally, but confidence is low because it provides only partial-r (0.0797) rather than PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS004944 is better supported for the target trait because it has higher endpoint fidelity (primary open-angle glaucoma / open-angle glaucoma with explicit POAG self-report phenotyping) and a much broader evaluation context (validated across multiple ancestries with a very large n=407,667), whereas PGS002761 is a generic “glaucoma” endpoint with EUR-only evaluation (n=39,444) from a cross-disease comparison paper. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect sizes and study/validation context: both have similarly strong per-SD ORs (1.74 vs 1.68), but PGS004944 is slightly stronger and comes with additional (though full-model) AUROC reporting under basic covariates, plus multi-ancestry GWAS composition, making it more likely to transfer well beyond EUR-only settings than PGS002761.

Both candidates target primary open-angle glaucoma, but PGS001792 has stronger PRS-comparable performance evidence: it reports a PRS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.03209, which is interpretable as PRS signal and is below the glaucoma liability h2 ceiling (~0.0556), whereas PGS004944 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC (0.748) plus an OR=1.74 without clarifying PRS-only discrimination. PGS001792 also uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with far more variants (911k vs 144k), and its evaluation includes a large European validation (n=347,396) with basic covariates; PGS004944’s endpoint is self-reported and its evaluation ancestry is listed as MAE-only, making transfer to a generic glaucoma benchmark less certain despite a slightly larger n.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported/phenotyped endpoint (lymphocytic thyroiditis mapped to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100% with AFR/HIS/EUR listed), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and covariates are unknown for both—so endpoint fidelity and study context do not differentiate. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best available tie-break is within-family empirical strength: PGS005271 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349). Variant counts are essentially identical and not decisive. Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported on the visible performance/effect-size evidence.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful for Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and consistent phenotyping_reported). However, PGS001254 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely small variant set (11 SNPs), which is a warning signal for generalization despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R² reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; R² 0.0247). PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a denser penalized-regression score (2443 variants) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability evidence than EUR-only evaluation in PGS001254. Given the framework-penalty and very sparse architecture of PGS001254, PGS001880 is more likely to transfer better in an external benchmark.

PGS000643 is mapped to the correct EFO (follicular lymphoma) and, despite the reported/phenotyping label being “Nodular lymphoma,” it provides a much more fully specified and likely higher-signal genome-wide PRS (PRS-CS; 1,048,780 variants) with basic, non-leaky covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs) and includes PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.133; top 1% vs rest OR 2.49) plus pseudo-R². In contrast, PGS002304 has perfect endpoint wording (Follicular lymphoma) but is an extremely sparse 6-variant GWS score with unknown covariates and only a full-model AUROC reported (0.61) on a very small validation set (n=197), which is not a PRS-comparable metric and is less reliable for benchmarking. Given both lack PGS-only AUC/R², the structural advantage and richer PRS-specific evidence favor PGS000643.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), publication family, evaluation ancestry mix, and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the small full-model AUROC edge for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.630) is not a reliable differentiator. In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, structural signals and effect-size strength matter more: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.55, β≈0.44) than PGS005270’s very weak effect (OR≈1.04, β≈0.04) from a 55-variant P+T score. That combination makes PGS005271 better-supported as a standalone PRS likely to transfer better externally.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=18,971), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are method/structure and the selected partial-correlation: PGS002092 uses genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2) with far more variants (484,484 vs 2,443 for PGS001880’s penalized regression sparse model) and has a slightly higher partial-r (0.0797 vs 0.0783). Given identical study context, the more genome-wide model with marginally better performance evidence is better-supported.

PGS001792 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance evidence and validation context: it reports a PRS-only (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R2=0.03209 in EUR validation (n=347,396), which is below the glaucoma liability h2 ceiling (~0.0556) and thus sanity-consistent. PGS002761 has endpoint alignment (generic glaucoma) and a strong per-SD OR=1.68, but provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and has a much smaller validation sample (n=39,444). Both use basic covariates and similar PRS-CS family methods; given the lack of comparable metrics for PGS002761, the explicit PRS-only R2 plus much broader validation support makes PGS001792 the more reliably benchmark-competitive choice despite its framework-style publication context.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both Gout; trait_efo=gout), study family (same Am J Hum Genet benchmarking paper), training cohort/size (UKB, n=6,704), covariates (0), and evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) with the same validation N (90,274). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best differentiators are within-family performance and structural method signals. PGS004160 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) shows consistently stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence than PGS004018 (lassosum.CV): higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.678), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.073), and higher OR per SD (2.05 vs 1.93). Additionally, MultiPRS (ensemble/multi-score aggregation) is a positive structural signal versus a single-method lassosum score. The advantage is modest and based on full-model metrics, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_efo Hashimoto’s thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), publication family, evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%), and validation size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not decisive). In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, structural signals and effect-size strength matter more: PGS005272 uses PRSCS with genome-wide coverage (1,085,142 variants) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.42) than PGS005270 (OR≈1.04), which is consistent with better standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS005270 has a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.639 vs 0.605), that difference is small and not PRS-comparable given unknown covariates, so PGS005272 is better-supported overall.

PGS000997 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence for diverticular disease: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC (0.591) and PRS-only R² (0.0178) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array) and a multi-ancestry evaluation set (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), giving interpretable standalone PRS performance. PGS004544 has an endpoint-aligned ICD10 K57 phenotype and a large genome-wide variant set, but provides no AUROC/R² at all and only a modest OR=1.32 with unknown covariates; additionally, its “risk factor metaPRS” framing raises packaging/augmentation uncertainty without metrics to isolate PRS contribution. Given the benchmark goal (likely external performance ranking), the cleaner, directly comparable PRS-only metrics and broader evaluation context make PGS000997 the safer pick despite its pan-trait UKB framework origin.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/phenotyping (Hodgkin's disease), same EFO mapping (Hodgkins lymphoma), same publication/study family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training size (n=736), same validation size (n=775), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-only metrics and must rely on within-family performance/effect-size differences. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger signals than PGS000638: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). Given identical endpoint and covariate context, these consistent advantages support PGS000639 as the better-supported score.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication/study family (HGG Adv method-comparison), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are tiny performance/effect-size differences: PGS005083 has a marginally higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75358) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.455 vs 1.452) than PGS005077. These differences are very small, so confidence is low, but they favor PGS005083.

PGS002728 is from a disease-focused osteoarthritis study with a clinically anchored endpoint (phenotyping_reported: total hip replacement) and multi-cohort development (EB, GARP, HUNT, LLS, MyCode, UKB, arcOGEN, deCODE), which is generally more reliable for external transfer than a pan-trait UKB framework score. PGS000967 comes from the known high-throughput “813 traits in UK Biobank” sparse framework (snpnet) and uses a time-to-event coxarthrosis endpoint; despite reporting clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.561, R² 0.00628, below the h2 ceiling), those metrics are modest and the framework archetype is a consistent negative signal for real-world ranking when a disease-focused alternative exists. PGS002728 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC 0.66 with age/sex), lowering comparability, but its endpoint fidelity and study archetype advantage outweigh PGS000967’s modest PRS-only performance evidence.

PGS004236 is from a disease-focused, multi-cohort, explicitly multi-ethnic hypertension study (BioMe/MVP/UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation and reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.1 per SD), which is meaningful evidence of discriminative signal even without PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS001320 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as systematically weaker for external transfer; its clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649) are modest and do not clearly outweigh the framework/transportability penalty. Although PGS004236’s reported AUROC is full-model (and covariate-influenced), its endpoint alignment and disease-focused multi-cohort design plus strong OR make it more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the UKB framework sparse model.

Both candidates are near-clones: same endpoint (Graves’ disease; strong match to hyperthyroidism), same method (PRSCS), essentially identical variant counts (~1.085M), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and validation N (94,651), same publication and unknown covariates, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With design/context effectively tied, the small within-family performance edge favors PGS005265: slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger effect size (OR per SD 1.63 vs 1.54; β 0.486 vs 0.434). Differences are modest, hence low confidence.

The two candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication/study family, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=31,804), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (only full-model C-index). In this same-context tie, PGS005083 has marginally stronger empirical signals: slightly higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75325) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.455 vs 1.443). These differences are small, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS005083 over PGS005076.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (congestive heart failure), same method (LDpred), identical variant count (1,286,612), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same cohorts (MVP) and same validation size/ancestry context. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model C-index/AUC is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric. With everything else effectively tied, PGS005077 has a trivially higher full-model C-index (0.75358 vs 0.75325) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.452 vs 1.443), so it is marginally better-supported, but the differences are so small that confidence is low.

PGS002763 has the cleaner endpoint match for the target trait: phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis,” aligning with trait_reported/trait_efo, whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can introduce non-disease factors (surgical indication/access) and is less faithful to generic hip OA. Neither model reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002728’s full-model AUROC=0.66 (with age/sex) is not a comparable PRS metric and shouldn’t outweigh endpoint fidelity. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants and provides a moderate per-SD OR=1.38 (1.31–1.46), supporting meaningful PRS signal; PGS002728 is a sparse 44-variant GWS score with no effect-size evidence shown. Both are EUR-only evaluation; despite PGS002728’s multi-cohort development list, the proxy endpoint plus lack of PRS-comparable metrics makes it less well-supported for hip osteoarthritis risk than PGS002763.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context (same publication/family, same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin’s disease, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort MGI with n=736, same covariates age/sex/batch/PCs1-4, same validation size n=775) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only a weak tie-break. In this same-context comparison, PGS000638 shows slightly stronger validation signals: higher full-model AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0193 vs 0.013), plus a higher per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). Although PGS000637 uses PRS-CS with many more variants, the observed performance/effect-size evidence in the identical setting favors PGS000638.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Commun paper with identical trait/phenotyping (prevalent hypertension), identical covariates, same training N (10,314) and same evaluation sample size/ancestry (MAE 100%, n=39,035). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, and their full-model AUROCs are essentially identical (0.764 vs 0.763), so performance doesn’t differentiate. In this tie context, PGS004236 has stronger supporting evidence via an explicit PRS effect size (OR=2.1 per SD, 95% CI 1.99–2.21) and a more externally oriented development context (includes MVP in training/development cohorts) plus a larger genome-wide variant set (398,805 vs 234,228), making it the better-supported choice than PGS004234, which lacks effect-size reporting and has a narrower cohort list.

PGS002763 is the better-supported choice for the target trait hip osteoarthritis because it has cleaner endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported exactly “Hip osteoarthritis” vs PGS000967’s time-to-event “TTE coxarthrosis”), uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS with 1,052,273 variants) that is structurally better aligned to polygenic architecture than the very sparse snpnet model (634 variants), and it reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, 95% CI 1.31–1.46) that provides direct PRS signal evidence despite missing AUC/R2. PGS000967 does provide explicit PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.561, R2=0.00628) that are below the heritability ceiling and thus plausible, but it comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework archetype and its PRS-only performance is modest; its multi-ancestry evaluation listing does not outweigh the framework/sparse-model penalty given the stronger endpoint match and structural properties of PGS002763.

Both candidates are near-clones: same gout endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (6,704), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (90,274), and both report only full-model (not PGS-only) AUROC/R² with covariates listed as 0. In this same-context comparison, PGS004047 has consistently stronger reported performance and effect sizes than PGS004018 (full-model AUROC 0.685 vs 0.678; R² 0.0801 vs 0.0734; OR per SD 2.00 vs 1.93), and it also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (865,644 vs 100,595), which is a supportive structural signal when endpoints and covariates match. Because neither provides PRS-only metrics, confidence is not high, but the within-family performance/effect-size edge favors PGS004047.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same reported/phenotyped endpoint (“Nodular lymphoma” mapped to follicular lymphoma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI), same training N (3,696), same validation N (3,256), and identical basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; full-model AUROC differences are small and likely noise. In this tie-like setting, PGS000644 has slightly stronger overall discrimination/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.538 vs 0.532; per-SD OR 1.149 vs 1.133; pseudo-R² 0.00349 vs 0.00282) and a larger genome-wide variant set (2,209,179 vs 1,048,780), so it is marginally better-supported than PGS000643 despite PGS000643’s higher top-1% vs rest OR.

PGS004234 is from a hypertension-focused, multi-ethnic study explicitly about hypertension prevalence/progression with multi-ancestry development and evaluation (BioMe + UKB; diverse DEV ancestries and MAE evaluation), which is a positive transportability and study-archetype signal versus PGS001320 coming from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) that domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models in external validation. Although PGS001320 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.629; PGS R2 0.0649, below the h2 ceiling) and PGS004234 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a covariate-influenced full-model AUROC 0.763 with additional epidemiologic covariates like BMI/smoking), the framework penalty and weaker external-transport archetype for PGS001320 outweigh its metric availability. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (hypertension), with PGS004234’s ‘prevalent hypertension’ still a direct disease endpoint.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Hodgkin's disease”), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohorts (MGI), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; full-model AUROC differences are only meaningful within this same-context sibling comparison. In that setting, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000637: higher AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), stronger per-SD OR (1.476 vs 1.3), and higher top-1% OR (2.64 vs 1.67). Despite PGS000637’s more genome-wide method/variant count (PRS-CS; ~1.0M variants), the observed validation metrics in the same evaluation context favor PGS000639.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (Gout), same EFO, same publication/family, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (6,704), same eval ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) and validation N (90,274), and both have covariates listed as 0 with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model metrics). In this like-for-like setting, the small but consistent performance edge favors PGS004160: higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.685), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.080), and slightly stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 2.05 vs 2.00; β 0.717 vs 0.693). With endpoints and covariate context effectively identical, these within-family metric/effect-size differences are the best available tie-break, so PGS004160 is better-supported than PGS004047.

PGS005265 is better-supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease) is a clinically dominant subtype of hyperthyroidism and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-biobank global study with broad external evaluation (AllofUs, MVP, FinnGen, UKB etc.) and multi-ancestry validation (selected validation ancestry includes African American/LatAm/European; eval MAE 100%) plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.63), suggesting meaningful PRS signal even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not reported. PGS001043 is an exact-label match (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and reports clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.6323; R2 0.0216, below the h2 ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants, UKB-only development) which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external transfer; its modest PRS-only performance does not clearly outweigh the disease-focused multi-cohort evidence and stronger effect-size signal in PGS005265.

PGS005266 is the better-supported choice for the target trait hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease) is a clinically dominant and tightly aligned subtype of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation context (validation n=94,651; evaluation across African American/LatAm/European). It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.54), which is meaningful evidence of PRS signal even though only a full-model AUROC is shown. In contrast, PGS001043 is an snpnet score from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” framework (a systematic underperformer archetype for external transfer), with a very sparse 69-variant model and only modest PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6323; PGS-only R2 0.0216) that do not clearly outweigh the framework penalty despite exact label match. Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort design plus strong effect-size evidence makes PGS005266 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the UKB sparse framework score.

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are the broad JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly restricted to the oligoarticular subtype (endpoint mismatch for a generic JIA target). Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and EUR-only development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so PGS000325’s higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.738) is not enough to outweigh the broader endpoint fidelity advantage of PGS000114 for this target.

PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,114) and reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (HR 2.34; OR per SD 1.33; plus high-vs-median-tertile OR 5.9) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, reducing risk of covariate-driven inflation. PGS000739 is a sparse 27-variant genome-wide-significant score and its only visible discrimination metric is a full-model AUROC (0.821) built with heavy clinical covariates including multiple comorbid risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making the AUROC largely non-comparable to PRS-only performance. Both have aligned HCM phenotyping, but the cleaner covariate context and stronger polygenic construction favor PGS004911 despite both lacking explicit PGS-only AUC/R2.

PGS005218 is better-supported as a standalone hypothyroidism PRS candidate because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with explicit incident hypothyroidism phenotyping and a much richer multi-cohort development context (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) plus very large evaluation (n=441,692). PGS002766 is from a cross-disease “family history vs PRS across 24 diseases” framework-style paper with sparse per-trait metadata (training N/A, single UKB cohort) and only an OR (1.47 per SD) with no discrimination metrics. Although PGS005218 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.859) that is likely inflated by heavy thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) and thus not PRS-comparable, PGS002766 provides even less direct performance evidence and has weaker overall study support; therefore PGS005218 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks despite the covariate-leakage concern.

PGS000114 has the best endpoint fidelity to the target trait (phenotyping_reported and trait_efo are the broad juvenile idiopathic arthritis), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype (RF-negative polyarticular JIA), which is a mismatch for a generic JIA target absent evidence it is the dominant form. Both are from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and EUR-only development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.738 vs 0.76) are not decisive. As a tie-break within this near-clone family, PGS000114 also shows a materially stronger reported effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51), supporting stronger PRS signal despite PGS000326’s larger validation N.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same disease-focused paper (same method SparSNP, EUR-only dev/eval, same covariates sex+PCs, similar training/validation sizes), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only full-model AUROC plus per-SD OR. With endpoint fidelity to the broad target (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) being comparable (both are JIA subtypes), the best differentiators are the within-family performance/effect-size signals: PGS000325 shows higher AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.93 vs 1.51), plus more variants (21 vs 12), all pointing to stronger discriminative signal than PGS000326 in the same evaluation context.

PGS004908 is better-supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) and shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 1.5 per SD, 1.43–1.58) with a much larger variant set (107 vs 19). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and only report full-model AUROC (0.74 vs 0.722), which is not a reliable cross-model PRS comparator; given that, the stronger per-SD effect size and disease-focused study archetype favor PGS004908 over PGS000076, which is from a cross-cancer evaluation and shows weaker PRS association (HR 1.16, 1.08–1.26) despite similar covariate adjustment and EUR-only evaluation.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all = hypothyroidism) and both are UKB-developed/evaluated in EUR only, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so we fall back to structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002766 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (1,092,122 vs 6,127 for PGS004935), which is a positive structural signal for a polygenic disease when PRS-only metrics are absent. Effect sizes are very similar (OR 1.47 for PGS002766 vs OR 1.50 for PGS004935), and PGS004935’s reported AUROC=0.70 is a full-model metric (not PRS-only) with unknown covariates, so it cannot be used as a decisive PRS-quality advantage. Given comparable endpoints and similar ORs, the stronger methodological/coverage profile supports PGS002766.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,883), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. In this same-publication, same-endpoint setting, the best differentiators are the directly comparable performance proxy and structural properties: PGS002031 has slightly higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.1355 vs 0.1307 for PGS001823) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with a much larger variant set (6,713 vs 654), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal when other fields are matched. The partial-r difference is modest, so confidence is not high, but the combined metric + variant-count edge supports PGS002031.

PGS005218 is better-supported overall for hypothyroidism because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with much broader multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), a far larger evaluation sample (n=441,692 vs n=8,417), and a genome-wide shrinkage approach with very large variant coverage (1,110,091 vs 6,127). Although both candidates only report full-model AUROC (no PRS-only AUC/R2), PGS005218’s reported AUROC=0.859 is heavily confounded by explicit thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making it non-comparable as PRS evidence; however PGS004935 is a portability/framework-style UKB-only score with sparse SNPs and limited validation context, and its AUROC=0.7 is also not PRS-only and lacks covariate transparency. Net: despite covariate leakage concerns in PGS005218’s metric, its endpoint is still aligned (incident hypothyroidism) and its study/design signals are substantially stronger than the UKB-only portability score PGS004935.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and evaluation context: same trait/EFO (kidney cancer/renal cell carcinoma), same phenotyping (incident kidney cancer), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates, same validation sample size (n=391,610), and essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.722; C-index ~0.723–0.724) and HR per SD (1.16 for PGS000076 vs 1.15 for PGS000787). Candidate_b (PGS000787) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, which is a structural red flag rather than added evidence of better PRS signal, and its reported R²=0.366 appears to be a full-model/other metric (not PRS-only) and is implausibly high relative to the provided kidney-cancer heritability ceiling, making it non-comparable for PRS ranking. With no clean PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the original, directly specified score (PGS000076) is better-supported than an inverted-weight derivative (PGS000787).

PGS004562 is better aligned to the generic target of kidney failure: its phenotyping is ICD code N18 chronic renal failure (a direct kidney-failure endpoint), whereas PGS000708 is explicitly phenotyped as “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a narrower subtype that is a mismatch for a generic kidney-failure benchmark. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back to structural/effect-size evidence: PGS004562 shows a stronger per-SD effect (OR 1.395) than PGS000708 (HR 1.19), and it uses a metaPRS-style integration approach with much larger genome-wide variant coverage (1,059,939 vs 183,272). PGS000708’s reported C-index 0.779 is a full-model metric with covariates and is not comparable as PRS performance, so it doesn’t outweigh the endpoint mismatch and weaker effect size.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS000739’s higher AUROC (0.821) is heavily discounted because its covariates explicitly include multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status (HCM-ACMG), which is strong clinical/mediator packaging and can inflate discrimination unrelated to the PRS. In contrast, PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), making its reported effects (e.g., HR 1.97; OR 1.26 per SD; OR 5.5 high vs median tertile) more indicative of standalone PRS signal. Structurally, PGS004910 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with 374,190 variants versus PGS000739’s 27 GWAS-significant variants, which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal in external benchmarks when endpoint fidelity is equal. Overall, cleaner covariate design plus genome-wide construction outweighs the covariate-inflated full-model AUROC advantage of PGS000739.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (N18 chronic renal failure) mapped to kidney failure, same publication (Commun Biol), same training cohort (UKB) and training N (174,489), same EUR-only development/evaluation, same variant count (1,059,939), same validation N (56,192), and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available effect-size evidence: PGS004562 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.39548) than PGS004492 (1.1708), suggesting stronger PRS discriminative signal in the same endpoint family. Method differences (RFDiseasemetaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here, but the stronger observed OR in PGS004562 breaks the tie in its favor.

PGS004908 is better-supported for the target trait because it is a disease-focused kidney cancer GWAS meta-analysis score with substantially stronger PRS signal (OR per SD 1.5 [1.43–1.58]) and a much richer variant set (107 genome-wide significant SNPs) than PGS000787 (19 variants; HR per SD 1.15 [1.07–1.24], suggesting weak PRS discrimination). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the similar full-model AUROCs (0.74 vs 0.722) are not decisive and are likely covariate-influenced; in that setting, the stronger effect size and more direct disease-genetics study archetype favor PGS004908 over PGS000787, which comes from a pan-cancer risk-factor integration framework and reuses/inverts weights from another score.

PGS002729 is the better-supported knee osteoarthritis PRS because it is clearly disease-focused with a direct clinical osteoarthritis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: knee osteoarthritis / clinical osteoarthritis) and transparent basic covariates (age, sex, BMI), plus an explicit validation AUROC reported (0.66, with CI) in Europeans. In contrast, PGS004549 comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (title: integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS), has unknown covariates (raising comparability/packaging concerns), provides no discrimination metrics (no AUC/R2), and only a moderate OR (1.37) as performance evidence. Despite PGS004549’s much larger genome-wide variant count and larger training/validation N, the weaker metric transparency and higher likelihood of packaged prediction make it less reliably supported for standalone knee OA PRS performance than PGS002729.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication, same late-onset AD endpoint (familial LOAD), same method (21 genome-wide significant variants), same covariates (age, sex), and same development cohorts, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. The main differentiator is the available PRS-discrimination proxy: PGS000054 reports a materially stronger per-SD odds ratio (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR=1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is a strong tie-break within the same endpoint family. Although PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-only evaluation, validation size is a weak signal here and does not outweigh the much stronger effect-size evidence favoring PGS000054.

Both candidates are near-clones: same target EFO/phenotyping (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), same publication, method (PRS-CS), EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), same development cohorts and validation N (343,182). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (full-model AUROC is not a PRS-comparable metric), the best differentiators are within-family performance/effect-size signals and any endpoint-enhancing framing. PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced variant (a mild positive per domain guidance) and shows consistently stronger reported metrics in the same setting (full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5), so it is better-supported than PGS004910.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease), but PGS000054 has cleaner PRS-relevant evidence: it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), which is a meaningful discriminator when PRS-only AUC/R² are absent for both. PGS000054 also has transparent, basic covariates (age, sex) and a broad disease-focused multi-cohort development context, whereas PGS000334 provides only a full-model/unspecified R²=0.191 with unknown covariates—this magnitude is suspect for a C+T score and is not PRS-comparable, especially given the low heritability ceiling noted in the context. Validation sample sizes are similar (3,324 vs 3,810) and do not outweigh the stronger, cleaner PRS signal evidence in PGS000054.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. However, PGS004860 has stronger structural PRS properties (LDpred2 with ~1.14M variants vs PGS000078 genome-wide significant hits with 109 variants) and a stronger per-SD effect size signal (OR=1.33 vs HR=1.16), suggesting more standalone PRS discrimination. PGS000078’s evaluation is much larger but its reported performance is heavily packaged with extensive non-genetic predictors (family history, detailed smoking variables and interactions, PM2.5), making its high full-model AUROC less informative about PRS quality than PGS004860’s simpler covariate set.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo=osteoarthritis, knee) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be separated by comparable metrics. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS002767 is a broad cross-disease comparison paper, whereas PGS004549 comes from a disease-prediction study explicitly integrating disease PRS with risk-factor PRS (a multi-score aggregation signal that is generally favorable structurally). Their per-SD ORs are very similar (PGS002767 OR=1.35 with CI; PGS004549 OR≈1.367), so effect size doesn’t favor A. With similar EUR-only evaluation, PGS004549 also has larger stated training (n=174,489) and validation (n=56,192 vs 39,444), providing slightly stronger support overall despite unknown covariates.

PGS000328 is better aligned to the target trait as a direct systemic lupus erythematosus score evaluated in a dedicated SLE-focused context, whereas PGS000196 is framed as prioritizing an SLE diagnosis among rheumatology outpatients with inflammatory arthritis (a more context-restricted/triage phenotype). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.83 for PGS000328 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are not strong cross-study differentiators, but they are at least consistent with PGS000328 not being weaker. PGS000328 also has broader validation support (n=1,001 vs n=245) and a slightly larger SNP set (57 vs 55), while PGS000196’s mixed-ancestry evaluation is not enough to offset its more specialized endpoint framing.

PGS004492 is the better-supported match to the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is cleaner: phenotyping_reported is ICD-10 N18 (chronic renal failure), aligning directly with kidney failure, whereas PGS000708’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure in all,” a narrower subtype that is a mismatch for generic kidney failure. Neither model provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we fall back on structural and effect-size signals: PGS004492 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with ~1.06M variants (stronger polygenic capture) versus PGS000708’s snpnet multi-PRS with 183k variants, and their per-SD effect sizes are similar (OR 1.17 vs HR 1.19), offering no advantage to overcome PGS000708’s subtype restriction. PGS000708’s reported C-index 0.779 is full-model (not PRS-only) and thus not a reliable cross-model discriminator.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (incident lung cancer; EFO lung carcinoma), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same variant count (109), same covariate-heavy risk-factor integration (includes family history, smoking variables/interactions, PM2.5), and essentially identical reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, which is a strong negative structural signal versus the original directionally consistent construction in PGS000078. The extra R²=0.799 reported in PGS000789 is a generic/full-model R² (not PRS-only) and is also implausibly above the lung-cancer liability h2 ceiling (~0.15), so it does not provide credible evidence of superior PRS signal. With near-clone context otherwise, the original score (PGS000078) is better-supported than an inverted-weight derivative.

Both candidates target systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported/trait_efo) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the visible AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Candidate_a (PGS000328) has a notable endpoint restriction in phenotyping_reported (onset before age 20), which is a pediatric/early-onset subset and less faithful to the generic target trait “lupus erythematosus” than candidate_b’s generic SLE phenotyping. With performance metrics not PRS-comparable, structural signals matter more: candidate_b uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with far more variants (293,684 vs 57), which is generally more likely to capture polygenic signal and transfer better than a small GWAS-hits score. Although PGS000328 shows a higher full-model AUROC (0.83 vs 0.65), that advantage is discounted because it is full-model and paired with a restricted early-onset endpoint; thus PGS000754 is better-supported for the broad SLE target.

Both candidates align well to the target (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R², so performance can’t be directly compared on PRS-comparable metrics. PGS000053 is better-supported by a clearer, cleaner evidence package: it reports an OR=1.29 (1.21–1.37) as a PRS effect-size signal and uses only basic covariates (age, sex), with a broad multi-cohort disease-focused development list and EUR evaluation. PGS000334 reports only a full-model/unspecified R²=0.191 with unknown covariates (raising comparability concerns and potential inflation), and lacks effect-size evidence; its GWAS ancestry is also partly non-reported. Given the absence of PRS-only metrics in both, the combination of explicit PRS effect size + cleaner covariates favors PGS000053.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. The key differentiators are structural PRS strength and covariate packaging: PGS004860 is a genome-wide LDpred2 score with 1,143,554 variants (stronger polygenic signal capture), and its evaluation uses relatively standard covariates (age/sex/BMI/smoking status/PCs). PGS000789 is a small 109-variant score (inverse-weighted from another PGS) embedded in a heavily packaged risk-factor model including family history, detailed smoking intensity/duration interaction terms, and PM2.5, making its high full-model AUROC/C-index largely non-informative about standalone PRS quality. Given the absence of PRS-only metrics for both, the genome-wide LDpred2 construction and cleaner covariate context make PGS004860 more likely to rank higher in external PRS benchmarks than the sparse, risk-factor-integrated PGS000789.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are identical: incident lymphocytic leukemia; covariates are the same basic set), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak differentiator. In this near-clone setting, PGS000788 shows consistently stronger outcome association/performance in the same EUR evaluation context: higher full-model AUROC (0.738 vs 0.719), higher C-index (0.756 vs 0.735), and notably higher HR per SD (1.70 vs 1.45). With variant count and evaluation sample size also essentially matched (75 variants; n=391,338; EUR eval), the stronger HR and slightly better discrimination support PGS000788 over PGS000077.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo are identical), but PGS002767 has cleaner endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported (explicit “Knee osteoarthritis”) versus PGS002729’s broader “Clinical osteoarthritis,” which is less knee-specific. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002729’s full-model AUROC=0.66 (with age/sex/BMI) is not a comparable PRS metric and is likely covariate-influenced. In the absence of PRS-only metrics, PGS002767 provides a directly PRS-informative effect size (OR per SD 1.35, moderate signal) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; 1,052,275 variants) that is structurally better suited to polygenic architecture than PGS002729’s 24 genome-wide significant hits. Both are EUR-evaluated; the larger validation N for PGS002767 (39,444 vs 14,926) is only a weak tie-break but is directionally supportive.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. Given that, PGS000077 is better-supported structurally and empirically: it uses many more variants (75 genome-wide significant hits vs 6 P+T SNPs in PGS000645), shows a stronger per-SD effect size (HR=1.45 vs OR=1.358), and is developed across multiple cohorts with a very large European evaluation sample (n=391,338 vs n=957). PGS000645’s evidence package is weaker overall (very sparse score, small dev/validation context), and its lower full-model AUROC (0.578 vs 0.719) cannot rescue it because these are covariate-influenced metrics.

Both candidates target systemic lupus erythematosus and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC), so the AUROC values (0.65 for PGS000754 vs 0.79 for PGS000196) are not cleanly comparable as PRS performance. Endpoint fidelity favors PGS000754: its phenotyping_reported is a direct SLE endpoint, whereas PGS000196 is explicitly framed as “SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis,” a more context-restricted outpatient/arthritis setting that may not transfer as a general lupus erythematosus PRS. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural signals break the tie: PGS000754 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant count (293,684) versus a sparse P+T score with 55 variants for PGS000196, which is generally less robust for polygenic disease risk. PGS000754 also has a substantially larger validation sample (7,733 vs 245), providing more stable evidence even though validation size is only a weak tie-break.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication (Br J Dermatol external evaluation), same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not strong cross-model PRS comparators).
