Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and context: same trait (melanoma), same phenotyping_reported (incident invasive melanoma), same basic covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication family, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not ideal for PRS ranking). In this same-study, same-endpoint setting, the small but consistent performance edge favors PGS002246 (full-model AUROC 0.688; R² 0.07) over PGS002253 (AUROC 0.662; R² 0.051). Method/structure also slightly favors PGS002246 (50 genome-wide significant variants vs 45 in the updated-weights prior PGS), while PGS002253’s much larger validation N is a weak tie-break signal per guidance and doesn’t outweigh the within-family discrimination gap.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration), use the same method (PRS-CS), have identical evaluation ancestry (EUR) and validation sample size (n=163,011), and use the same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10), so this is a near-clone comparison where within-family performance/effect-size differences are informative. PGS004606 shows stronger reported discrimination and PRS signal in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.71; OR per SD 1.76 [1.73–1.78]) than PGS004607 (AUROC 0.65; OR 1.48 [1.34–1.63]). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the materially higher OR and AUROC in the same evaluation context favors PGS004606; additionally, its GWAS ancestry (EUR) matches the EUR evaluation better than PGS004607’s AFR-only GWAS, which is a transportability disadvantage when both are evaluated in Europeans.

PGS000788 is better supported for the target lymphoid leukemia because it uses a substantially richer PRS (75 variants vs 6 for PGS000645) and shows a stronger PRS effect size signal (HR per SD 1.7 [1.53–1.88] vs OR per SD 1.358 [1.113–1.657] for PGS000645), which is a more reliable indicator of PRS discriminative power when PRS-only AUC/R² are absent for both. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (incident lymphocytic leukemia vs lymphoid leukemia), and covariates are similarly basic (age/sex/PCs/array/batch), so the large gap in full-model AUROC (0.738 vs 0.578) is not treated as a decisive PRS-only metric but is directionally consistent with the stronger effect size for PGS000788. PGS000645’s very small development/training scale (n=1,100) and extremely sparse 6-variant P+T construction further weaken its likelihood of ranking higher in external benchmarks compared with the more substantial, multi-cohort-derived score used in PGS000788.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and structure: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma), same method (genome-wide significant variants), same variant count (23), and same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (PGS002306: 0.69 vs PGS002281: 0.644) is not a reliable PRS discriminator, especially since covariates differ/are unclear. PGS002281 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, geographic region) and also provides an additional PRS-relevant effect-size signal (OR highest vs lowest quintile = 3.18), whereas PGS002306 lists covariates as unknown and provides no supporting effect size. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the better-supported record is PGS002281, but confidence is low because the two are otherwise extremely similar and PGS002306’s higher full-model AUROC could reflect real differences we cannot attribute to the PRS alone.

PGS004606 is a disease-focused, endpoint-faithful score for age-related macular degeneration (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all align) developed in an AMD consortium context (IAMDGC) with basic covariates only, and it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.76), which is supportive of meaningful PRS discrimination. PGS001013 comes from a pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”), with a broad/less specific phenotype label (“Eye problems/disorders Macular degeneration”) and very weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC≈0.553; R2≈0.006), consistent with limited standalone PRS signal; its higher full-model AUROC is likely covariate-driven and not comparable. Despite PGS004606 lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, its stronger endpoint fidelity and disease-focused study archetype plus strong OR make it more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the sparse framework score.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Br J Dermatol external evaluation study, with identical trait/endpoint alignment (melanoma; incident invasive melanoma), identical basic covariates (age, sex), and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry; neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers. Within this same-endpoint/same-covariate context, PGS002247 shows materially better reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.691 vs 0.662; R² 0.072 vs 0.051) and also uses a slightly larger GWAS-hits set (68 vs 45 variants), supporting stronger captured signal. PGS002253’s much larger validation N is a weak signal and does not outweigh the consistent performance advantage for PGS002247 in the comparable evaluation setting.

PGS004607 is the better-supported choice for the target trait because it is a disease-focused AMD score with high endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all explicitly age-related macular degeneration) and shows strong PRS signal via an OR per SD of 1.48 (near the “strong” threshold) using only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). In contrast, PGS001013 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-PRS framework (“813 traits”), with a very small 53-variant model and weak PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.553; PGS-only R2 0.006), consistent with limited standalone PRS discrimination despite clean reporting. Although PGS001013 has explicit PRS-only metrics and multi-ancestry evaluation, its framework origin and low PRS-only signal make it less likely to rank highly than the disease-focused, genome-wide PRS-CS AMD model (PGS004607), even though PGS004607 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and reports only a full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same publication, with identical endpoint fidelity (MI PheCode 411.2; trait_efo myocardial infarction), identical covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distributions, and same validation sample size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model C-index is only a weak tie-break. In this otherwise matched context, candidate_b (PGS005045, PRS-CS) has marginally stronger reported performance and effect size (full-model C-index 0.78385 vs 0.78336; OR per SD 1.554 vs 1.541), so it is slightly better-supported than PGS005035.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). However, PGS002038 comes from a UKB “portability of 245 scores” framework-style paper and reports only a weak PRS-comparable metric (partial-r=0.0396) with no AUROC/R2/effect-size evidence, despite large training/validation; such framework scores are empirically less reliable for external ranking when a disease-focused alternative exists. PGS000809 is disease-focused (MS risk variants from multiple MS cohorts/IMSGC-style development), uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), and provides at least some discrimination/effect-size signal (full-model AUROC 0.765; β=0.63), making it the better-supported choice on visible fields even though its AUROC is not PRS-only.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple myeloma (matching trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores in EUR-only evaluation, with only full-model AUROC reported (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so metrics are only weakly comparable. Given that, PGS002281 has the stronger observed validation signal in the visible record: higher full-model AUROC (0.644 vs 0.577) and a stronger stratification effect (OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 vs PGS000653’s OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1). PGS000653 also comes from a repository/framework-style paper (Cancer PRSweb) and shows only modest pseudo-R² (0.0145) with no PRS-only isolation, whereas PGS002281 is from a disease-focused multiple-myeloma PRS paper with similarly basic covariates. Overall, PGS002281 is better-supported on performance/effect-size evidence without added leakage signals.

The two candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same method (ldpred), same variant count (1,286,612), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=30,379). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index is only a weak within-family tie-break. On the selected European validation record, PGS005039 is marginally stronger than PGS005035 on both full-model C-index (0.7848 vs 0.7834) and per-SD OR (1.578 [1.50–1.67] vs 1.541 [1.46–1.63]), so it gets the edge, but the differences are small, hence low confidence.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with similar variant counts (PGS002306: 23 vs PGS000653: 22). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002306 (0.69) is not a reliable cross-model PRS discriminator, especially with covariates listed as Unknown. PGS000653 is better-supported on visible design/interpretability fields: it provides explicit basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), reports PRS-associated effect sizes (OR per SD 1.327) and additional metrics (Nagelkerke R², Brier, top-1% OR), and has documented training/development context (UKB; samples_training n=3,377) with a larger validation sample (n=2,738 vs n=290). Overall, PGS000653 has a more complete and comparable evidence package, while PGS002306’s apparent advantage rests mainly on a non-PRS-only AUROC with unspecified covariates.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all multiple sclerosis) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparability is limited. PGS002726 is from a disease-focused MS susceptibility/phenotype study (IMSGC-based) and provides stronger disease-relevant evidence (AUROC 0.80 reported plus a very large risk gradient: OR top 10% vs median = 15.0), whereas PGS002038 comes from a UK Biobank portability framework paper and only reports a small partial correlation (partial-r = 0.0396), which is weak as a standalone PRS signal. Despite PGS002038 having larger training/validation and explicit basic covariates, the framework/portability archetype and weaker effect metric make it less likely to rank higher than the disease-focused MS score.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (benign nodular goiter) with identical ancestry/validation context (MAE eval; n=94,651; same multi-biobank study family; covariates unknown), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are weak evidence. Under the fallback guidance, structural/effect-size signals dominate: PGS005262 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.41, β≈0.34) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T 110-variant score with weak effect (OR≈1.05, β≈0.05). This combination makes PGS005262 better-supported and more likely to transfer as a stronger PRS.

Both candidates are endpoint-aligned to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a clean cross-model PRS comparator. However, PGS000809 has stronger support on study design transparency and transportability: it reports basic covariates (age, sex, PCs) and is developed across many MS GWAS cohorts with a much larger evaluation sample (n=8,370), whereas PGS002726 has unknown covariates, a small evaluation (n=938), and its very large variant count is inconsistent with the stated 'genome-wide significant variants' method label, reducing interpretability. With comparable endpoint fidelity and no PRS-only metrics, PGS000809’s clearer covariate context and broader multi-cohort development/validation make it more likely to rank higher externally despite slightly lower full-model AUROC.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/efo and phenotyping_reported all indicate benign nodular goiter) and come from the same multi-cohort study with identical evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC). With endpoint and validation context essentially tied, structural and effect-size evidence favors PGS005263: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants versus PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants, and it shows a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.36 vs 1.048). The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.5876 vs 0.5854) is negligible, so the stronger PRS construction and effect-size signal make PGS005263 better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical endpoint fields (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Tobacco use disorder; trait_efo = nicotine dependence), identical training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), identical basic covariates, and the same validation sample size (n=19,400), so the decision rests on within-family performance and structural signals. PGS002037 shows stronger reported PRS signal in the selected record (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (847,691 vs 13,838), which is generally favorable for polygenic traits when other fields are matched. PGS001830’s sparse penalized regression and lower partial-r provide less support here.

PGS005235 is more endpoint-faithful to the target trait obesity: despite the broader trait_reported label (“Adiposity”), its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Obesity (phecode: 278.1)” with trait_efo=obesity, whereas PGS002033 uses a broader administrative bundle phenotype (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”) and comes from a UKB portability/framework-style paper. Both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, but PGS005235 provides supportive PRS discrimination evidence via a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.97), while PGS002033 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079) that is harder to interpret as standalone PRS performance. Covariates are similarly basic in both, so the decision is driven by better phenotype specificity plus stronger effect-size evidence for PGS005235.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same publication (HGG Adv), same endpoint (MI PheCode 411.2; phenotyping_reported myocardial infarction), same cohorts (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution, same validation size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005039 has slightly higher full-model C-index (0.78484 vs 0.78385) and slightly stronger OR per SD (1.578 vs 1.554) than PGS005045. These gaps are small, so confidence is low, but they consistently favor PGS005039.

PGS001273 is the better match to the generic target trait “osteoporosis”: its trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are straightforward osteoporosis case status, whereas PGS001274 is explicitly a restricted time-to-event endpoint (“osteoporosis without pathological fracture”), which is a narrower/horizon-style framing and less faithful to the broad target. Although both are near-clones from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework with identical training size, covariates, and evaluation context, and PGS001274 shows slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 and more variants, that performance edge is modest and comes with the endpoint mismatch. Hence PGS001273 is preferred, but confidence is low because the two records are otherwise extremely similar and PGS001274’s PRS-only metrics are somewhat stronger.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; EFO Nasal Cavity Polyp), publication/study family (same Commun Biol paper), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), variant count (1,059,939), and they lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and have unknown covariates—so performance must be inferred from the remaining comparable evidence. The main differentiator is effect size: PGS004535 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.60) than PGS004465 (1.35), which is a meaningful signal of stronger PRS discrimination within the same endpoint/study context. Although PGS004465 uses LDpred2 (a strong shrinkage method), within same-family siblings the observed effect-size advantage is the more direct evidence, so PGS004535 is better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same phenotyping string, same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). In this near-clone setting, the small but consistent performance/effect-size edge favors PGS005262: higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and stronger effect sizes (OR 1.408 vs 1.362; β 0.342 vs 0.309). Variant counts are essentially identical, and while PGS005262 lists a slightly broader set of development cohorts (adds BBJ, CKB, MGI), that is a weak tie-break; the main differentiator is the modestly stronger observed signal in PGS005262.

PGS000549 is the better match to the target trait (ovarian neoplasm): its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to malignant ovarian neoplasm, whereas PGS003394 is narrower (epithelial ovarian cancer; trait_efo ovarian carcinoma) and its phenotyping_reported is explicitly a 10-year risk package (horizon-conditioned), which is a negative comparability signal for standalone PRS quality. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model C-index for PGS003394 (0.623 vs 0.567) is not decisive and may reflect non-comparable/unknown covariates; by contrast PGS000549 discloses basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch) and provides PRS-relevant effect sizes (OR per SD ~1.26). Overall, endpoint fidelity and cleaner evaluation context favor PGS000549, but confidence is low because both lack PRS-only metrics and PGS003394 has much larger, consortium-based development/validation.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same publication (Cancer PRSweb), with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: malignant neoplasm of ovary; trait_efo: ovarian neoplasm), identical ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (UKB) and size (n=5,130), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=5,196). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either, the small full-model AUROC difference is essentially noise; tie-break should rely on structural and within-family empirical signals. PGS000550 uses PRS-CS with genome-wide coverage (1,115,189 variants) and shows slightly stronger reported association/evidence (OR per SD 1.286 vs 1.263; Nagelkerke R2 0.0113 vs 0.00996) than the sparse GWAS-hits model PGS000549 (16 variants), making PGS000550 the better-supported choice.

PGS002033 is better-supported structurally for obesity risk: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (846,292 vs 9,227 for PGS001298’s sparse snpnet), and it is explicitly framed/evaluated in a portability context across multiple ancestries. While PGS001298 provides clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (AUROC 0.576; R2 0.011) and basic covariates, it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) and uses a time-to-event obesity endpoint, both of which are warning signals for external transfer. PGS002033 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial-r reported), lowering certainty, but given the strong method/coverage advantage and the portability-focused evaluation design, it is more likely to rank higher on external benchmarks than the sparse pan-trait TTE score.

PGS005235 is better-supported for the target trait obesity because its endpoint fidelity is a direct obesity diagnosis (phenotyping_reported: “Obesity (phecode: 278.1)”) despite the broader trait_reported label (“Adiposity”), whereas PGS001298 uses a time-to-event framing (“TTE obesity”), which is a known weaker/less comparable endpoint for generic obesity risk. Structurally, PGS005235 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (709,828), aligning with expectations for a highly polygenic trait, while PGS001298 is a sparse snpnet score with only 9,227 variants from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”), a study archetype that tends to generalize worse than disease-focused/multi-cohort development. Although PGS001298 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.576/0.011) that are plausible under the heritability ceiling, those metrics are modest and do not outweigh the combination of stronger endpoint anchoring and more appropriate genome-wide modeling in PGS005235; PGS005235 also provides supportive effect-size evidence (OR≈1.97 per SD) even without AUC/R².

PGS002768 is better-supported for osteoporosis risk despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2 because it comes from a disease-focused cross-disease evaluation study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (1,091,549) and a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) in a sizable EUR validation (n=39,444) with only basic covariates. In contrast, PGS001273 is a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a very sparse snpnet model (316 variants) with weak PRS-only performance (AUROC=0.5685; R2=0.00688), which is characteristic of poorer external transfer even though it reports clean PRS-only metrics and has large UKB training. Endpoint fidelity is similar (both phenotype ‘Osteoporosis’), so the framework-penalty plus much weaker PRS signal and sparse architecture make PGS001273 less likely to rank highly in external benchmarks than the genome-wide PRS-CS score.

Both candidates target the same endpoint concept (Pancreatic cancer; EFO exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same method/variant set (22 genome-wide significant variants) with the same listed development cohorts, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). Given that near-tie, PGS000083 has stronger supportive performance evidence in the visible fields: higher reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.745 with also a C-index 0.742) and a slightly stronger per-SD effect size signal (HR 1.49 vs PGS000663 OR 1.44). PGS000663 is additionally penalized on endpoint packaging because its phenotyping is explicitly horizon-conditioned ("0–10 years of follow-up"), and its covariates include diabetic status and other clinical/collection factors consistent with a risk-prediction package, making its AUROC less informative for standalone PRS ranking. Therefore PGS000083 is better-supported for the target trait.

Both candidates target the same endpoint concept (Pancreatic cancer; EFO exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and both are sparse 22-variant GWAS-hit style scores with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so full-model AUROC is not a clean differentiator. PGS000663 is from a pancreatic-cancer risk-prediction study and shows broader evaluation ancestry (EAS+EUR) with a comparable per-SD effect size (OR 1.44), whereas PGS000794 is a pan-cancer risk-factor integration package with heavier covariate packaging including family history of multiple cancers and smoking intensity, making its higher full-model AUROC/C-index less informative about the PRS itself despite a similar HR (1.49). Given the benchmark goal of standalone PRS transfer, the less risk-factor-integrated, more disease-focused framing of PGS000663 is slightly better-supported, but the decision is close due to near-matched variant count and effect sizes and lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

PGS000550 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (ovarian neoplasm) because its endpoint is a direct malignant ovary neoplasm diagnosis (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Malignant neoplasm of ovary”, trait_efo matches ovarian neoplasm) with transparent, basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs) and it reports PRS-relevant effect sizes (OR per SD 1.286) alongside evaluation metrics. In contrast, PGS003394 has a partial concept mismatch (trait_efo ovarian carcinoma rather than ovarian neoplasm) and, more importantly, its phenotyping is packaged as “10-year ovarian cancer risks,” which is a horizon-conditioned risk wrapper that is less comparable to generic disease status; covariates are also unknown, making its higher full-model C-index (0.623 vs 0.568) hard to interpret as PRS strength. With neither candidate providing clean PRS-only AUC/R2, the cleaner endpoint fidelity and covariate transparency favor PGS000550 despite PGS003394’s larger training/validation scale and multi-ancestry evaluation.

PGS000903 is better-supported as a standalone PD PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis (Lancet Neurol; multiple PD cohorts listed) with a substantially richer polygenic model (1805 variants, C+T) and reports meaningful PRS discrimination evidence via a strong extreme-quantile OR (top vs bottom quartile OR=6.25) alongside basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). PGS003763 is a very sparse 44-SNP genome-wide-significant score from a frailty/incident-PD risk-factor study context, with no training details and only a modest tertile HR=1.72; its incident-only framing and limited PRS evidence make it less likely to rank highly in external PD PRS benchmarks despite the larger evaluation N.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Lancet Neurol PD GWAS meta-analysis with identical phenotype alignment (Parkinson’s disease), covariates (PCs 1–5, age, sex), training cohorts, training N, and the same validation sample size (n=999), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is only a weak tie-break). In this same-study sibling comparison, PGS000903 is better-supported: it uses a richer C+T construction with far more variants (1805 vs 90), reports stronger full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.692 vs 0.651), and provides additional supportive effect-size evidence (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25 and R² 0.054) that PGS000902 lacks. Given identical endpoint/covariate context, these combined signals favor PGS000903 as more likely to rank higher externally.

PGS000902 is better-supported as a standalone Parkinson disease PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis (multiple PD consortia/biobanks listed; training n=1,473,098) and uses a larger GWAS-hit set (90 variants vs 44). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, but PGS000902 at least reports a (covariate-adjusted) AUROC=0.651 with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), whereas PGS003763 provides only a time-to-event HR (1.72 high vs low tertile) from an incident-PD frailty-focused study context with no training details (samples_training N/A), making its PRS strength and construction less directly supported. Despite PGS003763’s large evaluation N, that is a weak tie-breaker versus the stronger disease-GWAS development evidence for PGS000902.

Both candidates are near-clones: same prostate cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (9,671), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (171,474), and both report only full-model (not PRS-only) AUROC/R² with covariates listed as 0. In this same-context comparison, PGS004155 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) has consistently stronger reported discrimination/effect size than PGS004139 (SBayesR-auto): higher full-model AUROC (0.7049 vs 0.7003), higher R² (0.1280 vs 0.1213), and higher per-SD OR (2.166 vs 2.109). Given the domain guidance that multi-score aggregation is a positive structural signal and that within-family performance differences can break ties, PGS004155 is better-supported.

PGS002768 is the better-supported choice for generic osteoporosis risk because its endpoint is a direct osteoporosis phenotype (phenotyping_reported: "Osteoporosis") and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (~1.09M), plus it reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) under basic covariate adjustment. In contrast, PGS001274 comes from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (snpnet; 813 traits) and uses a time-to-event, narrower endpoint ("osteoporosis without pathological fracture"), which is a fidelity mismatch for the broad target; its PRS-only metrics are explicitly modest (PGS-only AUROC≈0.576, R²≈0.009), and the high full-model AUROC (0.797) is largely covariate-driven given the small incremental AUROC (0.0078). While PGS001274 has larger training N and multi-ancestry evaluation, the framework+sparse-method and endpoint framing make it less likely to rank highest in external benchmarks than the more disease-aligned, genome-wide PRS-CS score.

PGS002046 is the stronger pick on structural grounds: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (570,308) and comes from a portability-focused evaluation explicitly spanning multiple ancestries, which is generally more compatible with capturing polygenic signal than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001255 (213 variants) from the “813 traits” pan-trait framework that is flagged as prone to poorer external generalization. While PGS001255 has clean PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.6319; R2 0.01341, below the heritability ceiling), its endpoint is explicitly time-to-event (“TTE otosclerosis”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic otosclerosis target, and its framework origin plus extreme sparsity weakens confidence in transfer. PGS002046 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial-r=0.0182), so confidence is low, but given the framework penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001255, PGS002046 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking.

Both candidates are near-clones: same prostate cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (9,671), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=171,474), and both report only full-model AUROC/R² (no PRS-only metrics) with covariates listed as 0. The performance gap is tiny, so confidence is low, but it slightly favors PGS004139.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping (“Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”), identical training size (n=391,124), covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), and identical multi-ancestry evaluation mix and validation N (n=19,668), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so performance evidence is limited to the selected partial correlation. In that like-for-like setting, PGS002055 has slightly stronger reported PRS signal (partial-r 0.0175 vs 0.0151 for PGS001843) and is also a genome-wide shrinkage score with far broader variant coverage (599,514 vs 242), which is a favorable structural signal for a complex disease endpoint. Given the otherwise matched context, these two advantages make PGS002055 the better-supported pick, though confidence is only moderate because the metric gap is small and both are framework-derived scores.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target peripheral vascular disease because it is a disease-focused PAD score with a clear clinical endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (1,296,292), and provides meaningful PRS signal via effect size (HR per SD 1.66). It is also evaluated broadly across multiple ancestries with a large validation sample (n=304,294), suggesting stronger external robustness. In contrast, PGS001843 comes from a UKB portability/framework study (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”), is a very sparse penalized-regression score (242 variants) for a vague/unspecified PVD phenotype, and its only comparable performance evidence is a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0151), consistent with weak PRS signal. Neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger endpoint specificity + effect-size evidence + disease-focused archetype favor PGS005217.

PGS001280 is the better-supported match to the target trait pulmonary embolism because its endpoint is PE-specific (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: "PE (time-to-event)" / "TTE PE"), whereas PGS001277 uses a composite phenotype ("PE +/- DVT") that is less faithful to PE alone. Although PGS001277 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R² and incremental AUROC, the performance gap is small and does not outweigh the clearer phenotype alignment of PGS001280 for a PE-only benchmark setting.

Both candidates are near-clones: same prostate cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication/study family, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (9,671), same evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS) and validation N (171,474), and both list covariates as 0 with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model metrics). PGS003587 is better supported for the target trait (preeclampsia) because its endpoint fidelity is stronger: despite a broader trait_reported label (“Gestational hypertension”), its phenotyping_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia,” aligning directly with the target, whereas PGS004593 has an exact trait_reported (“Preeclampsia”) but phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” a closer mismatch to the target endpoint. Both use the same method (PRS-CS), similar genome-wide variant counts, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size and study context matter more; PGS003587 shows a slightly stronger per-SD association (OR 1.20 vs HR 1.16) and comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort Nat Med study with explicit training cohorts and training N reported, while PGS004593 has N/A training size and no listed development cohorts. PGS004593’s larger validation N is only a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the endpoint mismatch in phenotyping_reported.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping (psoriasis), identical training cohort/size (UKB n=391,124), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), identical ancestry evaluation mix, and the same validation sample size (n=19,615), so endpoint fidelity and transportability context do not differentiate. Although PGS002083 uses many more variants and LDpred2, the within-family empirical performance shown is essentially tied and slightly favors PGS001871, so it wins on the only visible discrimination evidence.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to psoriasis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, so the decision hinges on PRS-comparable performance evidence and comparability. PGS001312 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC no covariates 0.6916 with CI; PGS R² no covariates 0.0523), with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array) and a larger evaluation sample (n=67,425). PGS002083 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r 0.0632) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength less directly supported on the visible fields despite a larger training set and many more variants. PGS001287 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence for psoriatic arthritis: it reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.676 and PGS R² 0.0335) with basic covariates only, and these are plausible under the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0735). In contrast, PGS000342 is disease-focused and endpoint-faithful but provides only a full-model AUROC (0.562) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its genetic predictive performance hard to compare and seemingly weaker on the available discrimination evidence.

PGS001277 is better-supported for a generic pulmonary embolism target because it provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.611 and PGS-only R²=0.015) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and it is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), improving evidence for transportability. In contrast, PGS003861 has tighter endpoint wording (PE only) and is disease-focused in Han Chinese, but it reports only a full-model AUROC (0.765) with unknown covariates and no PRS-only AUROC/R², making its apparent performance largely non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven; it is also EAS-only in both GWAS and evaluation, limiting generalizability evidence.

PGS003586 has markedly better endpoint fidelity to the target trait preeclampsia: its phenotyping_reported is “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia” and trait_reported matches, whereas PGS004593 maps to preeclampsia in trait fields but its phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either candidate, effect-size and study support matter more: PGS003586 shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31) than PGS004593 (HR 1.16), suggesting higher discriminative signal. PGS003586 also has clearer disease-focused multi-cohort development metadata (multiple biobanks listed, training n=212,034) versus PGS004593 with N/A training and no cohorts listed. PGS004593’s larger validation sample (n=138,317 vs 25,582) is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the phenotype mismatch and weaker effect size.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (Pancreatic cancer / exocrine pancreatic carcinoma; incident pancreatic cancer), ancestry (EUR eval), variant count (22), and covariates (including family history and smoking/BMI), and they show essentially identical full-model discrimination and effect size (AUROC 0.745; HR ~1.49). However, PGS000794 is explicitly constructed as “22 variants from Graff et al (PGS000083) with inverse variant weights,” which is a strong negative structural signal (it is effectively a sign-flipped version of the same score and thus not plausibly better-supported for the target trait). The extra reported R² in PGS000794 is not labeled PRS-only and is implausibly high relative to the trait heritability ceiling, so it does not provide credible advantage. Therefore the original, directly specified GWAS-hits score PGS000083 is better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Med paper, same method (PRS-CS), similar genome-wide variant counts (~1.09M), identical evaluation ancestry (EUR) and validation sample size (n=25,582), and the same phenotyping_reported endpoint (Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia) with the same basic covariates—so the main differentiator is endpoint fidelity and effect-size strength. PGS003586 is explicitly reported for Pre-eclampsia (matching the target trait) and shows a stronger per-SD association (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.24–1.38) than PGS003587 (OR 1.20, 1.14–1.26), which is reported as Gestational hypertension (a related but not identical label). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the stronger effect size plus closer trait_reported alignment makes PGS003586 better-supported.

PGS001030 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.6252 and PRS-only R²=0.0142 (and incremental AUROC=0.01818), which are interpretable and below the pulmonary fibrosis heritability ceiling, whereas PGS004695 provides no PRS-only AUC/R² and only an HR (high vs low quintile)=3.78 that is harder to benchmark across studies. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS004695 is idiopathic PF incident; PGS001030 is pulmonary fibrosis), but PGS001030 also has explicit training (UKB, n=269,704) and multi-ancestry evaluation listed, while PGS004695 is a small GWAS-hits score (23 SNPs) with N/A training details and EUR-only evaluation. Despite the framework-paper penalty for PGS001030, the presence of clean PRS-only metrics and clearer development/validation context makes it more likely to rank higher than the metric-sparse, very sparse GWAS-hit score PGS004695.

PGS001791 is better-supported for the target pulmonary fibrosis because it targets the clinically specific and closely matched endpoint idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all IPF) and comes from a multi-biobank global PRS development context with a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto; 910,439 variants), which is structurally more likely to transfer than a sparse pan-trait UKB framework score. Although PGS001030 reports higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only R2=0.0142; AUROC=0.6252) than PGS001791’s covariates-regressed-out R2=0.005929, PGS001030 is from the known ‘813 traits’ snpnet framework archetype (UKB-only development; 51 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically weaker in external generalization despite clean metadata. Both use only basic covariates, and both PRS-only R2 values are below the heritability ceiling, so the decision leans on endpoint fidelity plus study/method structure rather than the modest metric edge of the framework model.

PGS001137 has tighter endpoint fidelity to the target (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both exactly “Retinal detachment”) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663), which also passes the heritability sanity check (well below h2_obs≈0.0042 on the observed scale, i.e., not implausibly inflated). In contrast, PGS002040 uses a broader composite endpoint (“Retinal detachments and defects”) and reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.0276) with no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive strength less directly supported/comparable despite larger training N and a genome-wide LDpred2 construction. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates, so the decisive advantage is PGS001137’s clearer phenotype match plus explicit PRS-only metrics.

PGS004163 is better-supported for the target trait because its endpoint is a clinically specific RA subtype (phenotyping_reported: Seropositive RA) rather than the more deployment-/framework-oriented time-to-event framing in PGS004873 (phenotyping_reported: Incident RA) from a cumulative-incidence risk framework paper. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model metrics are not directly comparable; however, PGS004163 provides stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR=2.46 per SD) versus PGS004873’s HR=1.83, and it is evaluated in a broader context (EUR plus some SAS) with a much larger validation sample (90,274 vs 7,018). PGS004873’s higher full-model C-index (0.85) is discounted because it is not PRS-only and is paired with covariate adjustment (PCs 1–10), while PGS004163 lists covariates as 0, making its reported association less likely to be covariate-driven.

PGS000922 is the better-supported sarcoidosis PRS because it has clean PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.64282 and PGS-only R²=0.01741) with only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and its PRS-only R² is plausibly below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.107). In contrast, PGS001872 has a phenotype-mapping concern (trait_efo="skin sarcoidosis" vs target sarcoidosis) and lacks PRS-only AUROC/R², reporting only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0199) which is harder to benchmark against PRS discrimination. Although PGS001872 uses more variants and a larger training set, both candidates are UKB framework/portability-style scores, so the decisive advantage is PGS000922’s clearer endpoint alignment and directly comparable PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo (rheumatoid arthritis), same phenotyping_reported (Seropositive RA), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training size (n=820), same ancestry distribution, same empty covariates field (0), and same validation sample size (n=90,274). PGS004695 is a very sparse 23-SNP genome-wide-significant score from an exposure-focused incidence study and provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 (only an HR high-vs-low quintile), making its standalone PRS discrimination less directly supported and more sensitive to sparse-architecture underperformance. Validation sample sizes are similar and do not outweigh the stronger structural + PRS-metric evidence for PGS001791.

PGS001137 is better-supported on PRS-comparable performance for the target endpoint: it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.573 and PGS R2(no covariates)=0.00663), which are interpretable and pass the heritability-ceiling sanity check (h2_obs≈0.0042 is same-order; not an obvious inflation). PGS001833, while using a larger training set and a denser penalized-regression score (3737 variants), provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0218) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive strength less directly evidenced for benchmarking. PGS004049 is better supported for the generic target of rheumatoid arthritis because its endpoint is a direct clinical subtype match (phenotyping_reported: Seropositive RA) without time-to-event packaging, and it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR=2.37 per SD) alongside full-model metrics with no covariates (covariates=0), making the reported discrimination less likely to be covariate-inflated. Both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger effect-size evidence and cleaner covariate context favor PGS004049.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Carcinoma in situ of skin”), same publication family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI), same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation size (n=5,500). Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same method (PRS-CS), same ancestry context (GWAS EAS+EUR; EUR-only evaluation), and same basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/platform/batch), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family tie-break). Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same PRS-CS method, same basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch/array), and same EUR-only evaluation ancestry. Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping all match carcinoma in situ of skin), study family (same Cancer PRSweb paper), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), training size (n=6,005) and validation size (n=5,500). Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical training size (n=269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), ancestry setup, and validation size (n=67,425), and both report clean PRS-only AUROC/R² well below the sarcoidosis h2_liability ceiling (0.107), so heritability sanity-check passes for both. PGS005220 is better supported for the target trait because it targets the clinically dominant subtype (obstructive sleep apnea) with explicit OSA phenotyping and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation, whereas PGS003213 is an ExPRSweb framework score (UKB-only, EUR-only) that typically underperforms disease-focused models. Both candidates are near-clones: same obstructive sleep apnea endpoint (trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), same publication and method (PRS-CSs weighted summation), same covariates (including BMI), same training cohorts (FinnGen/MGBB/MVP), same evaluation ancestry and validation N, and both only report a full-model AUROC=0.79 (no PRS-only AUC/R2), so AUC cannot differentiate PRS quality. Both candidates are near-clones: same schizophrenia endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all schizophrenia), same publication, same method (PRS-CS), same GWAS/EVAL ancestry distribution, and same basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, platform/batch), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either record (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). Both candidates are endpoint-faithful (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all squamous cell carcinoma), EUR-only, trained in MGI with only basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). In this near-clone setting, PGS000461 has slightly stronger and richer performance evidence: higher per-SD OR (1.491 vs 1.4) and additional supportive metrics (top 1% vs rest OR=3.51; Nagelkerke R²=0.0304) with a marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.599 vs 0.59). PGS000120’s main advantage is larger validation N, which is a weak tie-break signal here, so PGS000461 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.599 in PGS000461 vs 0.605 in PGS000731) are not a reliable differentiator, especially with different/unknown covariates. PGS000461 is better-supported on visible PRS-relevant evidence: it discloses basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4) and provides additional performance context (Nagelkerke R², Brier score, top-1% OR), whereas PGS000731 has covariates listed as Unknown and fewer supporting metrics. Effect sizes are similar (OR per SD ~1.49 for PGS000461 vs 1.44 for PGS000731), so the richer, cleaner metadata package favors PGS000461 despite PGS000731’s much larger validation N.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same PRSweb paper with identical endpoint fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all thyroid cancer/carcinoma), identical training cohort (MGI), training N (4,481), validation N (4,270), and similarly clean basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this same-context comparison, PGS000630 shows slightly stronger overall discrimination evidence: higher full-model AUROC (0.626 vs 0.618), higher pseudo-R² (0.0393 vs 0.0365), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.598 vs 1.568). Although PGS000632 has a higher extreme-tail OR (top 1% vs rest 5.14 vs 3.53), the broader, more stable metrics favor PGS000630, and method/variant-count differences (GWAS hits 10 vs P+T 8) are minor here.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (“Thyroid cancer” mapped to thyroid carcinoma), same method (GWAS Hits), same variant count (10), same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same publication family—so small performance/effect-size differences are a legitimate tie-break. PGS000631 shows consistently stronger reported signals in the selected validation record (higher full-model AUROC 0.636 vs 0.626; higher pseudo-R² 0.0478 vs 0.0393; higher OR per SD 1.651 vs 1.598; higher top-1% OR 4.4 vs 3.53). PGS000630 has a larger training and validation sample and includes mixed EUR/MAE evaluation, but validation size/record_count are weak differentiators here and there are no PRS-only AUC/R² metrics for either model. Given the same endpoint/covariate framing, the stronger discrimination/effect-size package favors PGS000631.

PGS005219 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint is explicitly obstructive sleep apnea (the dominant clinical form of sleep apnea) with coherent phenotyping_reported = obstructive sleep apnea, and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (FinnGen, MGBB, MVP) with multi-ancestry evaluation. Although it only reports a full-model AUROC (0.79) rather than PRS-only metrics, it also shows a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.98), which is supportive of meaningful PRS signal. In contrast, PGS003213 is an ExPRSweb framework score (pan-trait repository archetype) with EUR-only training/evaluation and much weaker reported discrimination/effect size (full-model AUROC=0.527; OR=1.106), making it less likely to rank highly in external benchmarks despite having cleaner basic covariates.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS001297 is from a known pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, UKB-only development), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer despite clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.771, R2 0.091). PGS000024 comes from a disease-focused T1D study (T1DGC; newborn screening/incident diagnosis framing) and shows broader, multi-ancestry evaluation distribution, which is supportive of robustness; its very high reported AUROC (0.921) is full-model only and thus not directly comparable, but the overall disease-focused archetype and external-orientation outweigh the framework score’s modest PRS-only metrics. Therefore PGS000024 is more likely to rank higher in an external benchmark.

Both candidates match the target trait (T2D) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.793 for PGS002308 vs 0.852 for PGS001781) are not directly comparable PRS metrics and shouldn’t drive selection. Endpoint fidelity slightly favors PGS002308 because its phenotyping is generic “Type 2 diabetes” (fits a generic T2D risk target) whereas PGS001781 is explicitly “Incident type 2 diabetes,” which is a narrower time-to-event framing. Transportability evidence also favors PGS002308: it is explicitly trans-ancestry (PRS-CSx) with multi-ancestry GWAS input and very diverse evaluation ancestries, suggesting better cross-population robustness than PGS001781’s EUR-only GWAS base. Finally, PGS002308 shows a materially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.96 vs 1.52), which is a supportive discriminator when PRS-only metrics are absent.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS001297 is explicitly from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer despite clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.771, R2 0.0912; within the EUR heritability ceiling). PGS000023 comes from a disease-focused, ancestry-specific T1D study in African-ancestry participants with multi-cohort development and broad multi-ancestry evaluation, which is stronger transportability evidence than a single-biobank framework score. Although PGS000023 lacks PRS-only metrics (only a full-model AUROC 0.817, not directly comparable), its disease-focused design and multi-ancestry evaluation context outweigh PGS001297’s metric completeness given the framework penalty.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Squamous cell carcinoma”) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is only weakly informative. PGS000731 has slightly stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.605 vs 0.59; OR per SD 1.44 [1.41–1.48] vs 1.4 [1.31–1.5]) and a larger validation sample (88,924 vs 20,468). While PGS000120 has cleaner disclosed basic covariates (age/sex/batch/PCs) versus unknown covariates for PGS000731, there is no indication of heavy clinical leakage in either record; given the otherwise near-clone setup, the modestly stronger performance/effect-size signals and broader validation support favor PGS000731.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Thyroid cancer” / thyroid carcinoma), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and publication family, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics/effect sizes). In this same-context comparison, PGS000631 shows consistently stronger performance signals: higher full-model AUROC (0.636 vs 0.618) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0478 vs 0.0365), with a slightly higher per-SD OR (1.651 vs 1.568). PGS000632 has larger training/validation N, but domain guidance treats those as weak tie-breakers; the stronger discrimination/effect-size evidence favors PGS000631.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/EFO/phenotyping (“Cancer of bladder”), same method (GWAS Hits), same variant count (13), same EUR-only ancestry, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics shown, which are not PRS-comparable). With endpoints and design essentially identical, the small full-model AUROC difference (0.567 for PGS000611 vs 0.572 for PGS000610) is likely noise and not decisive. As a tie-break, PGS000611 has stronger risk stratification evidence (OR top 1% vs rest 2.66 vs 1.47) and slightly tighter per-SD effect estimate (OR 1.284 vs 1.292 but narrower CI), making it marginally better-supported despite similar overall evidence.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates. However, PGS001306 is explicitly a pan-trait UK Biobank framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse 179-variant snpnet model, which domain guidance flags as tending to generalize poorly despite having clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.630, R2 0.020). PGS004253 comes from a disease-focused UC study context (immune checkpoint inhibitor–mediated colitis paper) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575) plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.84), which is supportive of real PRS signal even though only full-model AUROC (0.66) is reported and thus not directly comparable as PRS-only. Given the framework penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001306, the better-supported likely-transferable UC PRS is PGS004253.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are type 1 diabetes) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not cleanly comparable PRS metrics. Given that, structural/study-support signals dominate: PGS000024 uses a much richer score (85 variants with interaction modelling) versus PGS000023’s very sparse 7-variant GWAS-hits score, which is less likely to capture polygenic signal. PGS000024 also shows broader evaluation ancestry distribution and a higher reported (though full-model) AUROC (0.921 vs 0.817). PGS000023’s AFR-only GWAS ancestry and extremely low variant count make it more niche/transport-limited despite its multi-cohort development list. Overall, PGS000024 is better-supported for general T1D risk prediction.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same PRSweb paper with identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all bladder cancer), identical EUR-only ancestry context, and the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC differences are essentially noise). In this tie-like setting, PGS000613 is better-supported: it has a stronger top-1% vs rest risk separation (OR 2.91 vs 1.47 for PGS000610) and a better Brier score (0.0821 vs 0.0917), with similar per-SD OR (~1.30) and similar full-model AUROC (~0.57). Method/structure also mildly favors PGS000613 (P+T with slightly more variants: 15 vs 13) without introducing extra covariate leakage.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus” mapped to urolithiasis), covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), training cohort/size (UKB, n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation size (n=19,913), so the decision rests on within-family performance and structural signals. PGS002075 shows higher PRS-comparable performance in the selected record (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (LDpred2, 731,196 variants) versus a much sparser penalized regression score (5,599 variants), which is generally favorable when other fields are identical. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the higher partial-r plus stronger genome-wide construction makes PGS002075 better-supported than PGS001864.

Both candidates have exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with only basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). PGS001306 is better-supported on directly PRS-comparable performance: it reports PRS-only AUROC=0.630 and PRS-only R2=0.02036 (and these are plausible under the provided heritability ceiling), whereas PGS001855 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) with no AUROC/R2, making cross-model benchmarking less direct. Although PGS001855 has larger training N and more variants, the lack of PRS-comparable discrimination metrics leaves weaker visible evidence than PGS001306’s explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and neither reports a clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on study archetype + PRS signal proxies. PGS004253 is from a disease-focused UC study and provides supportive PRS signal evidence via an OR per SD of 1.84 (strong discriminative signal) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), whereas PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability/framework paper and only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) with no effect-size evidence. Despite PGS001855 having larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation, the framework-origin + weaker metric proxy makes it less likely to rank highest in external benchmarks than the disease-focused, genome-wide shrinkage (LDpred2-auto, 744k variants) UC score in PGS004253.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication (Cancer PRSweb), with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), identical covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), identical EUR-only ancestry context, and the same training (UKB; n=12,992) and validation size (n=13,530). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; within this same-endpoint sibling comparison, the best available tie-break is the consistent (though small) advantage in reported discrimination/effect sizes for PGS000613: slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher pseudo-R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284). Given otherwise matched design, PGS000613 is better-supported.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to type 2 diabetes (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.793 for PGS002308 vs 0.8253 for PGS000805) are not decisive and are not directly comparable—especially since PGS000805 includes BMI as an extra covariate. PGS002308 has stronger structural support for a polygenic trait: a genome-wide shrinkage/trans-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with ~1.26M variants and explicitly diverse evaluation ancestry mix, plus a strong per-SD OR=1.96, suggesting robust standalone PRS signal. In contrast, PGS000805 is a sparse GWAS-significant-hits score (582 variants) and its strongest reported OR is a top-10%-vs-middle-20% contrast (2.95), which is less directly comparable to per-SD PRS strength. Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the more genome-wide, trans-ancestry PRS-CSx construction and directly interpretable per-SD effect size make PGS002308 better-supported for external performance.

PGS001864 has better endpoint fidelity to the target urolithiasis: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 is framed as “Calculus of kidney and ureter (time-to-event)” with trait_efo mapped to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis and a TTE endpoint (a mild mismatch/packaging penalty for a generic urolithiasis target). Both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, but PGS001864 shows broader multi-ancestry evaluation (including GME) and uses a much denser penalized regression score (5599 variants vs 341), which is a supportive structural signal for capturing polygenic signal. PGS001250’s advantage is having explicit PRS-only AUROC/R² (AUROC 0.5668; R² 0.00592), but these are modest and don’t clearly outweigh the endpoint alignment and structural advantages of PGS001864; however, because PGS001864 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R², confidence is low.

PGS001795 is the better-supported match to the target trait “uterine cancer” on endpoint fidelity and PRS-comparable performance: its trait_reported/phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Uterine cancer,” and it reports a PRS-only (covariates-regressed-out) Nagelkerke R²=0.001948, which is at least directly interpretable as PRS signal and is below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability≈0.0116), whereas PGS003381 targets the dominant subtype (endometrial carcinoma) but provides no PRS-only AUC/R² and only a full-model AUROC=0.761 that cannot be treated as standalone PRS performance. Although PGS003381 has a clean EUR-only GWAS/EVAL and basic covariates, the lack of PRS-comparable metrics makes its apparent AUROC advantage non-comparable; PGS001795’s framework-paper origin is a drawback, but it is outweighed here by the exact uterine-cancer endpoint plus an explicit PRS-only R² in a similar EUR evaluation setting.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its endpoint fields are coherent with the target (trait_reported vitiligo; phenotyping_reported explicitly “TTE vitiligo”) and it provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), and the PRS-only R2 is plausibly below the vitiligo heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported = “Red hair” despite trait_reported vitiligo), lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2, and only reports a pseudo-R2/full-model-style metric with unknown covariates, making its evidence less reliable for vitiligo risk prediction despite being disease-focused in publication title.

PGS002075 is the stronger pick for the target trait urolithiasis because it has cleaner endpoint fidelity (trait_efo exactly urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported are generic urinary calculus) and a structurally stronger genome-wide shrinkage construction (LDpred2 with 731,196 variants) with explicit multi-ancestry evaluation, which is supportive for portability. PGS001250, while it reports PRS-only AUROC/R2, comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse 341-variant snpnet model and a time-to-event endpoint (calculus of kidney and ureter), both of which are warning signals for external transfer; its PRS-only performance is also modest (AUROC ~0.567, R2 ~0.0059). Given the framework+sparsity penalties and endpoint packaging differences, PGS002075 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarking despite lacking an explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS because its endpoint is directly vitiligo (phenotyping_reported: TTE vitiligo) with clean PRS-comparable metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R²=0.01621), using only basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and a large EUR validation (n=67,425). Its PRS-only R² is also well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.174), making it plausible. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major endpoint mismatch: phenotyping_reported is anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients (therapy-induced, different disease), with no PRS-comparable AUC/R² and only an HR=1.41 from a small validation (n=1,584), making it much less reliable for generic vitiligo risk prediction despite the vitiligo label.

PGS001795 is better-supported for uterine cancer risk as a standalone PRS: it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.001948) in a very large European evaluation sample (n=170,276) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto; 911,692 variants). Its PRS-only R2 is also below the provided EUR heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; h2_liab≈0.0116), making it at least sanity-consistent. In contrast, PGS000541 is a sparse GWAS-hits score (18 variants) from a repository-style cancer PRS paper with much smaller validation (n=6,987) and lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2; its reported AUROC=0.576 is full-model and not directly comparable as PRS performance. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (uterine cancer / malignant neoplasm of uterus), so the decision rests on stronger PRS-isolated metric evidence plus more robust evaluation context favoring PGS001795.

PGS001781 is better-supported as a standalone T2D PRS: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally better suited to a highly polygenic disease than PGS000805’s 582 genome-wide significant hits. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown), so the small AUROC difference (0.852 vs 0.8253) is not decisive; however PGS001781 also reports a strong per-SD OR=1.52, providing direct PRS signal evidence, whereas PGS000805’s main effect metric is a top-10%-vs-middle OR (2.95) that is less comparable across settings. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS001781’s incident T2D framing is still a direct disease endpoint and its covariates are basic (no BMI), while PGS000805 includes BMI in the model, making its full-model AUROC more clinically covariate-influenced and less informative for PRS ranking.

PGS003381 is better-supported for the target uterine cancer because its endpoint is the clinically dominant subtype (endometrial carcinoma) with coherent phenotype fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all endometrial carcinoma) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant count (529,365), which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse GWAS-hits score in PGS000541 (18 variants). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not directly comparable PRS metrics; however, both use only basic covariates, and PGS003381’s much higher reported AUROC/R² (0.761/0.11 vs 0.576/0.0133) plus far larger evaluation sample (144,479 vs 6,987) provides supportive—though not decisive—evidence. PGS000541 has an exact umbrella label match (uterine cancer) and reports ORs, but its sparse construction and weaker reported discrimination make it less likely to rank highest externally.

PGS000738 is better aligned to the target trait vitiligo on the key endpoint-fidelity field: despite an odd phenotyping string (“Red hair”), its publication is explicitly about autoimmune vitiligo and the score is evaluated in a general EUR sample (n=4,702) with a PRS-relevant pseudo R² reported (0.0386), which is at least interpretable against vitiligo heritability. In contrast, PGS000760 has a clear endpoint mismatch in phenotyping_reported (anti–PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients), i.e., a treatment-induced, therapy-specific adverse event rather than vitiligo status; its reported HR (1.41) is tied to that non-vitiligo endpoint and thus is not reliable evidence for vitiligo risk prediction. With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R², endpoint fidelity dominates, favoring PGS000738.
